name: Banaras Tabla Gharana
tagline: A powerful, full-handed tabla school from Varanasi, shaped by Pandit Ram Sahai.
facts: Founder: Pandit Ram Sahai (1780 to 1826)
Part of the Purbi (eastern) baaj with Lucknow and Farukhabad
Suited to solo, khyal, dhrupad, kathak and thumri
Known players: Kishan Maharaj, Sharda Sahai, Samta Prasad
art: Banaras is one of the main tabla gharanas. It belongs to the Purbi baaj with the Farukhabad and Lucknow gharanas. It should not be confused with the Banaras vocal gharana.

Sources describe a powerful, resonant sound, although players can also be delicate. Resonant strokes such as Na (on the edge with the curved ring finger) and Din are central. Players prefer full-hand strokes. It works well as a solo and also for khyal, dhrupad and kathak, and suits lighter forms like thumri and tappa.
Mativetsky says Ram Sahai created forms such as uthan, the Benarsi theka and fard, and that the style uses over twenty compositional types.
artist: The gharana is traced to Pandit Ram Sahai (1780 to 1826), who trained in Lucknow under Modhu Khan and then developed the Benares style. The seven-night recital story is told in sources, but they give different ages for it.

The line runs through Bhairav Sahai (1815 to 1894) and Baldeo Sahai (1856 to 1906). Baldeo's sons and pupils include Kanthe Maharaj (1880 to 1969) and Bhagvati Sahai (1896 to 1946). Sharda Sahai (1935 to 2011) descends from Bhagvati and was a leading soloist and teacher.

Kishan Maharaj was born in 1923 in Kabir Chaura, Varanasi, and died in 2008. Wikipedia lists the Padma Shri (1973) and Padma Vibhushan (2002) for him; that page is flagged for weak references. He was taught by his father Hari Maharaj and then by Kanthe Maharaj. Other noted names are Samta Prasad (1921 to 1994), Anokhelal Mishra and Durga Sahai.
place: Varanasi, also called Benares or Kashi, is on the Ganga in eastern Uttar Pradesh. The gharana grew here and in surrounding mohallas such as Kabir Chaura.
The tabla here lived alongside kathak, thumri and temple music of the city. Players worked as accompanists as well as soloists.

history.what: Ram Sahai is born in 1780 in Varanasi.
He trains in Lucknow and then shapes the Benares style.
Ram Sahai dies; his line continues through Bhairav Sahai and Baldeo Sahai.
Baldeo's pupils, including Kanthe Maharaj, spread the style.
Kishan Maharaj is born in Kabir Chaura.
Kishan Maharaj and Sharda Sahai die.

future: Training: the guru-shishya line continues through teachers such as Sharda Sahai's students; wider teaching in schools would help.
Livelihood: concerts, accompaniment and teaching abroad give income; local stipends would help young players.
Materials: tabla makers and skin suppliers need steady support.
Documentation: record compositions such as uthan, fard and parans in notation and audio.
Protection: a Benares oral-history archive would help keep family teaching intact.

name: Baul
tagline: Wandering mystic singers of Bengal, with a one-string drone and songs of the body and the divine.
facts: UNESCO: inscribed in 2008, originally proclaimed in 2005 (Bangladesh)
Instruments: ektara, dotara, dubki
Songs said to date back to the 15th century
Joydev Kenduli Poush Mela in Birbhum draws many Bauls
art: Baul songs are the songs of wandering mystics of Bengal. UNESCO describes their poetry, music, song and dance as exploring the relationship between humanity and God, and the search for spiritual freedom. UNESCO says their devotional songs date back to the 15th century.

The songs draw on Hindu bhakti and Sufi ideas among others, but UNESCO says Bauls reject organised religion, the caste system and set places of worship. They see the human body as the place where God lives. Wikipedia adds that Lalon criticised religious divisions in his songs.

The main instruments, UNESCO says, are the ektara, a one-stringed instrument, the dotara, a lute, and the dubki, a drum. Wikipedia describes the ektara as a plucked drone made from a gourd, bamboo and goatskin, and the dotara as a long-necked, fretless lute, usually with four metal strings. Small cymbals (khartal, manjira), flutes and ankle bells also appear.
The singing is direct and the language is that of everyday Bengal. UNESCO notes that teachers pass philosophy to their disciples orally, and that the language of the songs is continually updated.
artist: Bauls are mystic minstrels, UNESCO says, a group long marginalised. Some live near villages and others travel from place to place, earning their living by singing. Wikipedia says that most are Sufi-influenced Bengali Muslims or Gaudiya Vaishnava Bengali Hindus, and that many came from lower-caste groups.

Lalon, also called Lalon Shah or Lalon Fakir, is the most celebrated Baul saint. Wikipedia gives his dates as 1774 to 1890, and notes other sources give 1775 to 1891. His shrine at Cheuriya near Kushtia, in Bangladesh, holds an annual gathering.

Purna Das Baul, born in 1933, is one of the best-known living Baul singers in India. Wikipedia says that President Rajendra Prasad recognised him as Baul Samrat in 1967. The claims about famous foreign admirers on the same page need a better source.
Teaching goes from guru to disciple by voice. Wikipedia notes that Islamists have targeted Bauls in some places, which is a real threat to this community.
place: Bauls live on both sides of the India-Bangladesh border. In India they are most closely linked to West Bengal, especially Birbhum district and Shantiniketan, where Rabindranath Tagore founded his school.

The Joydev Kenduli Poush Mela is held in Birbhum around Makar Sankranti, in the month of Poush, in honour of the poet Jayadeva. Wikipedia says so many Bauls attend that it is often called the Baul Fair. Bauls also gather at Shantiniketan during the Poush Mela.

UNESCO notes that the Baul tradition depends on the social and economic condition of Bauls, which has worsened in recent decades amid wider rural poverty in Bangladesh. The Bengal delta, with its rivers, villages and shifting settlements, has long been a home to wanderers.

history.what: UNESCO says Baul devotional songs date back to the 15th century. Scholars do not agree on an earlier origin.
Lalon lived in this span according to Wikipedia. Other sources give 1775 to 1891.
UNESCO says the Baul movement peaked in this period.
Rabindranath Tagore discusses the Bauls in lectures in Europe, and an essay from them appears in The Religion of Man (Wikipedia). Tagore's own songs show Baul influence.
Purna Das Baul is called Baul Samrat by President Rajendra Prasad (Wikipedia).
UNESCO proclaims Baul songs a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity (Bangladesh).
Baul songs are inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (Bangladesh).

future: Support Baul families with regular fees and health cover, since many live on small and irregular earnings.
Record songs from elders with the singer's own explanation, in Bengali and English.
Pay Baul singers fairly at Poush Mela, Shantiniketan and city festivals.
Protect singers against harassment and violence, and make their right to perform safe.
Help young people learn the ektara and dotara from living Bauls.
Treat Bangladeshi and Indian Bauls as one tradition in archives and festivals.

name: Bhakti Kirtan
tagline: Singing the names and stories of God together, with a leader calling and the crowd answering.
facts: Kirtan means narrating or reciting; group kirtan is sankirtan
Usually call and response, with drums and hand cymbals
Manipur's Sankirtana was inscribed by UNESCO in 2013
Found among Vaishnava, Warkari and Sikh communities, among others
art: Kirtan is devotional singing that tells and praises. The word comes from Sanskrit and means narrating, reciting or describing. Wikipedia says it is usually a group performance of call and response: a lead singer calls out a line and the others answer. Instruments often include the harmonium, tabla, mridanga and karatalas, small cymbals.

Kirtan grew in the bhakti movements, where devotion was open to people regardless of status or learning. Wikipedia names Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in 16th-century Bengal, Shankaradeva in Assam, and Vallabha's followers as promoting Krishna kirtan.

Forms differ by region. In Maharashtra, Wikipedia describes Warkari kirtan, which draws on saints such as Namdev and Tukaram, and Naradiya kirtan, which is performed by one person. In Sikh practice, shabad kirtan is the musical singing of the Guru Granth Sahib, usually in gurdwaras and set to ragas.

In Manipur, Sankirtana is a ritual of singing, drumming and dancing. UNESCO says a typical performance has two drummers and about ten singer-dancers, with devotees seated around them, and that it is seen as the visible manifestation of God.
artist: Kirtan has no single artist. It belongs to its performers, who may be lead singers, drummers and the whole gathered group. UNESCO says the knowledge of Sankirtana is passed from mentor to disciple, and that it marks festivals and life stages for the Vaishnava people of Manipur's plains.

In Maharashtra, the Warkari movement, whose sources name Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Chokhamela, Eknath and Tukaram among its poet-saints, sings kirtan and bhajan daily. Wikipedia says followers reject discrimination by caste, gender or wealth, and make a yearly pilgrimage to Pandharpur in the month of Ashadha.
The performers are often farmers, teachers and homemakers who sing in their spare time. Naming their individual voices is a task still to do.
place: Kirtan is heard all over India. Manipur's Imphal valley, where Sankirtana is performed in temple halls called mandapa, is one of its best-documented homes. Pandharpur in Maharashtra is where Warkari pilgrims gather. Wikipedia places Chaitanya's kirtan in Bengal, with Nabadwip as the usual centre, and Shankaradeva's in Assam. In Amritsar and elsewhere in Punjab, gurdwaras are the main places for shabad kirtan.
The pins show these places; their positions are approximate where marked. The form has also travelled abroad.

history.what: The Warkari movement forms in Maharashtra, with poet-saints such as Dnyaneshwar and Namdev, according to Wikipedia.
Bhakti teachers such as Chaitanya in Bengal and Shankaradeva in Assam spread group kirtan.
Wikipedia gives the 18th century as the start of the Meitei Sankirtana as it is now known; other sources point to earlier arrival in Manipur.
UNESCO inscribes Sankirtana of Manipur on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Kirtan is sung in temples, homes, gurdwaras and pilgrimages, and in yoga and devotional gatherings abroad.

future: Support mentor-to-disciple teaching in Manipur and elsewhere, with stipends for senior drummers and singers.
Record complete kirtans in each tradition, with texts, tunes and notes in the local language.
Make instruments such as the pung and mridanga easier to buy, repair and learn on.
Keep women and children involved, since the form depends on whole communities taking part.
Protect kirtan as a shared, community practice, and avoid reducing it to a show for visitors.

name: Bobbili Veena
tagline: A veena carved from one log of jackfruit wood, by families who have made it since the Bobbili court.
facts: Wood: jackfruit (panasa), one piece
Takes about a month to make
Makers: the Sarvasiddi families of Gollapalli
Geographical Indication, 2011 or 2012 (sources differ)
art: The Bobbili veena is a large plucked string instrument used in Carnatic music. It is carved from a single piece of jackfruit wood, so it is called an ekandi veena. The log is about four to five feet long.

The resonator, called the thumba, is traditionally a hollowed pumpkin, and may now be an aluminium bowl. A metal cylinder links it to the neck. Wikipedia gives a neck of about 51 inches and seven strings.

Makers say jackfruit wood is light, its grain suits the sound, and it swells little with moisture. Ivory inlay was once used, and plastic is used now because of the ivory ban. One veena takes about a month.
artist: The Sarvasiddi community of Gollapalli village near Bobbili has made the veena for generations. Outlook Traveller names Sarvasiddi Acchanna as the master craftsman appointed to the king's court. The South First says he is believed to have made the first Bobbili veena, under Pedda Rayudu.
The South First notes that Sarvasiddi Veeranna received a National Master Craftsman award in 1980. His son Sarvasiddi Ramakrishna says young people are not interested in the veena.
Players are called vainikas. Outlook Traveller says women played the veena especially in the Bobbili reign, and its style of playing is known as the Bobbili veena sampradayam.
place: Bobbili is a town in Vizianagaram district in north coastal Andhra Pradesh, about 55 km from Vizianagaram city. It was the seat of a small kingdom, and its rulers loved music.
Gollapalli, the village near Bobbili, is where the families who make the veena live. Sources count about 40 to 45 families.

history.what: Local tradition says the veena was first made in Bobbili under Pedda Rayudu, founder of the Bobbili kingdom.
Wikipedia says the instrument developed over more than three hundred years.
Sarvasiddi Veeranna received a National Master Craftsman award.
A crafts development centre was set up in Bobbili, which the South First says has not gained much traction.
The veena received a Geographical Indication tag. Wikipedia and the South First say 2011. I also saw 2012 in search results but did not open the source.

future: Teach young players in Bobbili and give them instruments, so makers have local buyers.
Help makers get wood legally and reliably, since jackfruit logs come through forest officials and traders.
Support the market for miniature veenas as an extra income, as Gollapalli families already make them, while protecting the full-size craft.
Document the making process and the Bobbili veena sampradayam style in recordings and measured drawings.
Use government and music-society purchases to give makers steady income.

name: Carnatic Music
tagline: South India's classical music, from the kriti of the Trinity to the December season in Chennai.
facts: Form: classical music of South India built on raga and tala
The Trinity: Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Syama Sastri
Main song form: the kriti
Chennai's December season began in 1927 to 1928
art: Carnatic music is the classical music of South India. Like Hindustani music, it is built on raga, a melodic frame, and tala, a rhythmic cycle. It is mostly vocal. Even when an instrument is played, the player tries to imitate the voice.

The main song form is the kriti, also called kirtanam. Wikipedia describes it as having three parts. The pallavi is a refrain of one or two lines, the anupallavi is a second verse, and the charana is the final and longest verse. Some kritis add a passage of sung notes (chittaswara), or a section sung at double speed.

A typical group has a lead singer, a violin following the melody, a mridangam drum for rhythm and a tambura drone. Wikipedia also lists the ghatam (clay pot), kanjira, morsing, flute, veena and chitraveena among the instruments that may join.

Alongside the composed song, musicians improvise. They explore the raga freely in alapana, and they sing kalpanaswaram, or improvised notes, within the rhythm. So a concert mixes learned songs and spontaneous play.
artist: The best-known composers are the Trinity. Wikipedia gives their dates as Tyagaraja (1767 to 1847), Muthuswami Dikshitar (1776 to 1835) and Syama Sastri (1762 to 1827). Wikipedia says they are honoured as a trinity for Syama Sastri's compositions, Dikshitar's varied output and Tyagaraja's many kritis. Dates of the composers are given differently in some sources.

Before them, Purandara Dasa (1484 to 1564 according to Wikipedia) is called the Pitamaha, the father or grandfather, of Carnatic music. He is said to have set the graded lessons that students still start with, including swaravalis and alankaras, and the raga Mayamalavagowla as the first scale.

Training is also teacher to student, traditionally in the teacher's home. Singers, violinists, mridangam players and veena players each train for years. Mridangam makers, who build the drum from wood and skin, are an essential but often unnamed part of the art.
I could not confirm from the sources I read the names of living artists to include. These need sourcing before adding.
place: Carnatic music grew across the four southern states, but its heart is the Kaveri delta in Tamil Nadu. Tiruvaiyaru is a town in Thanjavur district on the river Kaveri, about 11 km from Thanjavur city. Wikipedia says the name is linked to five rivers. It has the Aiyarappar temple, and Tevaram saints sang more than 100 songs about its deity.

Tiruvaiyaru is known for Tyagaraja, whose samadhi stands on the banks of the Kaveri. Every year the Thyagaraja Aradhana is held in the month of Margazhi (December or January), and leading Carnatic musicians gather there to sing his kritis.

The other great centre is Chennai (earlier Madras). The Madras Music Season was started in 1927, Wikipedia says, by the group that founded the Madras Music Academy. It was first held in March or April and from 1928 in December, for better weather and more visitors. Concerts are arranged by sabhas, such as the Madras Music Academy, Narada Gana Sabha and Indian Fine Arts Society, which also give titles and awards.
Temples, courts and homes in the delta fostered the art. Why this region became so rich in music is a question for historians, and I could not confirm a single explanation.

history.what: Purandara Dasa (1484 to 1564 in Wikipedia) sets out graded lessons that are still used to start teaching.
The Trinity lived in this span: Syama Sastri (1762 to 1827), Tyagaraja (1767 to 1847) and Muthuswami Dikshitar (1776 to 1835).
Tyagaraja lives at Tiruvaiyaru, where his samadhi now stands. The annual Aradhana honours him.
The Madras Music Academy is formally founded after a resolution at the All India Music Conference held with that year's Indian National Congress session in Madras.
The Academy holds its season in December, and the Madras Music Season takes its present timing.
Sabhas multiply in Chennai and become the main stage for concerts, with titles and awards.
The Madras Music Season is described as one of the largest cultural events in the world. The week-long Chennaiyil Thiruvaiyaaru festival is also part of the city's season.

future: Fund guru-shishya training for children from smaller towns, not only Chennai.
Give mridangam, violin and veena makers apprenticeships and fair prices.
Record Aradhana and season concerts with notes on raga and composer, and place them in open archives.
Take free concerts to delta villages and schools outside the December season, so musicians have year-round work.
Support women and artists from smaller communities with sabha slots and awards.
Teach the Trinity's songs in schools with translations.

name: Chenda Melam and Panchavadyam
tagline: Temple drum orchestras of Kerala, building from a slow start to a roaring finish.
facts: Panchavadyam: five instruments, four percussion and one wind
Chenda melam: all-percussion ensemble led by chenda drums
Heard at Thrissur Pooram, held in Medam
Panchavadyam form took shape in the 1930s per Wikipedia
art: A chenda is a two-headed drum with a jackfruit-wood body, played with sticks. Wikipedia says the left head has one or two layers of cowhide and the right head five or seven layers. The uruttu chenda leads and varies, and the veekku chenda keeps the basic beat.

A melam is a drum ensemble. Wikipedia lists Panchari, Champa, Chempada, Adantha, Anchadatha, Druvam and Pandi as melam types. Chenda melam is central to Kerala festivals, and the chenda also accompanies Kathakali, Koodiyattam and Theyyam.

Panchavadyam means an orchestra of five instruments. Four are percussion: timila, maddalam, ilathalam and idakka. The fifth is the kombu, a wind instrument. It builds a rising pyramid of tempo on the seven-beat thripuda thalam, with room for improvising on timila, maddalam and idakka. A big performance can use about 60 artists.
artist: Wikipedia credits Venkichan Swami and his disciple Madhava Warrier with shaping the modern five-stage panchavadyam concert in the 1930s, along with timila masters Annamanada Achutha Marar and Chengamanad Sekhara Kurup, and the idakka master Pattirath Sankara Marar. The article carries a warning about thin citations, so these attributions need checking.
The chenda craft is associated with Perumkollan smith families, and Vellarkad village is noted for instrument quality, per Wikipedia.
Formal training is offered at Kerala Kalamandalam, Kshetra Kalapeetham in Vaikom and Kshethrakala Kshethram in Kongad.
place: These ensembles belong to temple festivals in central and northern Kerala, mostly in March and April. Thrissur Pooram and Arattupuzha Pooram are named venues.

At Thrissur Pooram, Sakthan Thampuran, Maharaja of Cochin, is credited with starting the festival in 1796, according to Wikipedia. It centres on the Vadakkunnathan temple, with Paramekkavu and Thiruvambady sides. The Ilanjithara Melam begins at 2 pm on Pooram day, and Madathil Varavu is accompanied by a panchavadyam.

history.what: Chenda melam grows as a temple and festival tradition of Kerala.
Sakthan Thampuran is credited with starting Thrissur Pooram, per Wikipedia.
The elaborate form of panchavadyam takes shape, per Wikipedia.
Kalamandalam and other institutions teach it formally.

future: Keep training young drummers in both temple families and public schools.
Pay instrument makers and keep a supply of seasoned jackfruit wood and hides.
Record named melams with teachers, in notation and on video.
Look after hearing health for performers who play long festival hours.
Share festival income fairly with the artists.

name: Delhi Tabla Gharana
tagline: The oldest tabla school, said to be the source from which the others grew.
facts: Founder: Siddhar Khan Dhadhi, early 18th century
Style: bandh baaj (closed style), also called kinar baaj
Strong in qaida, rela and short compositions
Said to be the oldest tabla gharana
art: Tabla is a pair of hand drums used in Hindustani music. Each gharana has its own way of playing, its own stock of compositions and its own teachers. Wikipedia calls the Delhi gharana the oldest tabla gharana, and many writers call it the source of the others.

The Delhi style is called bandh baaj or closed style. Wikipedia contrasts it with the open style of Punjab and Farrukhabad. Outlook says its clarity comes from the early role of the tabla as accompaniment to song and instrumental music, and that the sharp sound comes from playing on the chanti or kinar, the rim of the right drum. Another name given is kinar baaj.

Wikipedia notes a large stock of qaidas, the basic theme and variation form, with light and precise strokes and bols such as dha and tita. A guide on hindustaniclassical.com lists qaida, rela, mukhda and mohra as its main forms, and says pakhawaj bols are not used. Sources differ in detail on these points, which is normal for an oral tradition.
artist: Siddhar Khan Dhadhi is the earliest known name. Wikipedia says he was a pakhawaj player of the tradition of Lala Bhavanidas. Outlook says he played at the court of Muhammad Shah Rangile. Accounts of his family and his origins differ, so these details should be read with care.

In the 20th century the main names include Natthu Khan (1875-1940) and Gamay Khan (1883-1958), described by Outlook as the most important player of the gharana in that century. His son Inam Ali Khan (1924-90) and disciple Latif Ahmed Khan (1941-90) carried it forward, along with Pandit Chatur Lal. Outlook names Ustad Faiyaz Khan, Ustad Rafiuddin Sabri and Pandit Subhash Nirwan as current exponents. Birth and death years vary slightly between sources.
place: The Delhi gharana is the tabla school named after the city. Sources place its start in the early 18th century, at the time of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah, known as Rangile. The Outlook article describes Delhi as a centre of music under many dynasties and patrons.

Its influence travelled outward. Wikipedia says players of this tradition founded or shaped other gharanas: Lucknow, Farrukhabad, Ajrara, Benares and Punjab. The Lucknow gharana is credited to Miyan Bakhshu, described as a nephew and disciple of the founder.
The Outlook article notes that the revolt of 1857 and the Partition of 1947 moved many artists away from Delhi in search of new patrons.

history.what: Siddhar Khan Dhadhi is credited with founding the gharana in Delhi, in the time of Muhammad Shah Rangile.
Disciples and relatives spread the tradition. The Lucknow gharana is credited to Miyan Bakhshu, and the Ajrara and others are linked to this lineage.
The revolt leads many Delhi artists to leave in search of patronage.
Natthu Khan and Gamay Khan are the leading names of the gharana.
Partition moves artists again.
Inam Ali Khan and Latif Ahmed Khan teach and perform.
Players such as Ustad Faiyaz Khan and Pandit Subhash Nirwan are named as current exponents.

future: Training: this is taught person to person by senior players, so support for the teaching families and for long-term students is the base.
Livelihood: accompaniment and solo concerts, and teaching in music colleges.
Materials: tabla making depends on skins, wood and iron-ring work. Keeping these craftspeople visible would help.
Documentation: record the compositions with named teachers and the line they were learnt from.
Protection: open sharing of old compositions with credit to the families who kept them.

name: Dhadi Singing
tagline: A small hourglass drum, a bowed sarangi and a story sung on its feet.
facts: Instruments: dhadd (small hourglass drum) and sarangi
A group (jatha) usually has 3 or 4 members
Sings vaars: heroic, devotional and folk ballads
Malwa was the main area, according to Hardial Thuhi
art: Dhadi is a Punjabi ballad tradition. The word names both the genre and the singers. Dhadis sing with the dhadd, a small hand-beaten hourglass drum, and the sarangi, a bowed lute.

Wikipedia says a jatha usually has three or four members: a sarangi player, one or two dhadd players, and a storyteller. They perform standing, sometimes singing together as a chorus, with chanted narration between sung parts.

The repertoire is wide. Hardial Thuhi, in the Journal of Punjab Studies, sorts folk dhadi tales into love stories such as Hir and Sohni, devotional tales such as Puran Bhagat, and heroic ones such as Dulla Bhatti. He also notes moral parables.
Because their texts do not come from scripture, Wikipedia says dhadi performances are not counted as shabad kirtan, though they are an important part of Sikh music.
artist: Thuhi writes that the Gurus used the word dhadi for one who praises God. He also writes that dhadi art as we know it began under Guru Hargobind (1606 to 1644), whose court dhadis were remembered as Natha and Abdul. The spelling and details vary between sources.

Thuhi says that in Malwa most dhadis came from Mirasi families, though people from other communities also made names. He names old masters such as Didar Singh Ratainda and Bhagatu Ramgarhia. Wikipedia lists present-day jathas such as those of Jaswant Singh Taan and Daya Singh Dilbar, and late artists Pal Singh Panchi and Sohan Singh Seetal. We did not check these living names beyond that page.
Dhadis were historically from lower castes, and the source says the work was not seen as respectable by higher castes.
place: Thuhi says dhadi singing was popular throughout Punjab but its main area was Malwa, quoting a saying that the dhadd-sarangi plays in Malwa.
Performances were held in village arenas, near ponds, at shrines and at gurdwaras. Sikh dhadis sing history in gurdwaras, especially around the Akal Takht in Amritsar (per Wikipedia).

history.what: The word dhadhi appears in the Guru Granth Sahib, where the Gurus call themselves dhadhi, a singer of praise.
Thuhi says Guru Arjan set some of the Gurus' vaars to the tunes of older warrior ballads.
Dhadi art flourished under Guru Hargobind, who is said to have kept dhadis to inspire his troops.
Thuhi says patronage faded after the death of Banda Singh Bahadur and the rise of the misls.
Folk tales began to be sung with dhadd-sarangi in peacetime, in the era of Ranjit Singh.
The first recordings of Punjabi folk balladry were made, including dhadi.
The tradition has shrunk under modern entertainment, but groups still perform in gurdwaras and fairs.

future: Pay dhadi jathas fairly for gurdwara and festival programmes.
Teach young players the sarangi and dhadd, which fewer learn now.
Record the long ballads (Hir, Puran, Mirza) in full before they are lost.
Document the lineages (gharanas) of Malwa through oral histories.
Include dhadi in school and university music programmes.

name: Dhrupad
tagline: The oldest surviving form of Hindustani music: slow, deep, and sung in praise of the divine.
facts: Form: the oldest surviving form of Hindustani vocal music
Begins with a long unmetred alap
Accompanied by the pakhawaj drum and tanpura
Family traditions include Dagar, Darbhanga and Bettiah
art: Dhrupad is an old form of Hindustani vocal music. Its name is linked by Wikipedia to the dhruvapada of the Natyashastra, though it notes that dhrupad's roots are much older. It is slow, serious and devotional, and many texts are in praise of gods, especially Krishna.

A performance opens with the alap, a long section where the singer explores the raga slowly, without rhythm and without words, using syllables such as nom and tom. Only after this does the composition begin, with the pakhawaj drum, a two-headed barrel drum, and the tanpura drone.
Wikipedia says the Dagar family style puts great emphasis on alap, and the family has often performed in pairs, frequently brothers. Voice is used with little ornament compared with khyal.
Dhrupad is also linked to a string instrument, the rudra veena. I did not confirm the details of this link in the sources read, so it is only mentioned here.
artist: The Dagar family is the best-known lineage, performing in the Dagar vani or Dagar gharana. Wikipedia describes them as Muslims who sing Hindu devotional texts, but that claim is marked as needing a citation.

Among the Dagar pupils are Umakant and Ramakant Gundecha, called the Gundecha Brothers, who come from Ujjain. They moved to Bhopal in 1981 to study dhrupad under Zia Fariduddin Dagar and his brother Zia Mohiuddin Dagar, and they set up a dhrupad institute outside Bhopal. They received the Padma Shri in 2012.

In Bihar, the Mallicks of the Darbhanga gharana are linked to the Khandar and Gauharvani styles. Pandit Vidur Mallick taught in Vrindavan in the 1980s and 1990s, and his sons Ram Kumar Mallick and Prem Kumar Mallick carried on the tradition. The Bettiah gharana is said to have flourished under the Bettiah Raj, with Pandit Falguni Mitra named as a present-day exponent, but those Bettiah claims need better sources.
Dhrupad singers need long years of voice training, and few students take up this hard and poorly paid path.
place: Dhrupad is tied to Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh. Wikipedia says Raja Man Singh Tomar, who ruled around 1486 to 1516, is linked with the form and with the Mankutuhal, and that a dhrupad school was set up at Gwalior. Ravi Shankar, cited there, says it grew from the older prabandha and flowered in Gwalior in the 15th century.

The tradition also looks to Braj, the land around Mathura and Vrindavan, and to the saints Swami Haridas, Surdas and Govind Swami. Haridas, a Krishna devotee and court musician linked with Gwalior, is a well-known dhrupad singer in Wikipedia's account, though its description of his relation to the Mughal court is confusing.

Under the Mughals, dhrupad was a court music. Wikipedia cites the Ain-i-Akbari (1593) as an early Mughal-era mention. After the courts declined, family traditions survived in Bihar's Darbhanga and Bettiah, and later teaching centres opened in places such as Bhopal.

history.what: The name is linked to the dhruvapada of the Natyashastra, but scholars say the roots of dhrupad are much older and the line of development is not certain.
Dhrupad flourishes in Gwalior under Raja Man Singh Tomar, who ruled about 1486 to 1516 according to Wikipedia.
Haridas and the Braj saints compose Krishna songs. The Ain-i-Akbari (1593) mentions dhrupad in the Mughal court.
Family schools including the Dagar and the Darbhanga and Bettiah gharanas develop under different patrons. Exact dates for these are not confirmed in the sources I read.
Pandit Vidur Mallick teaches dhrupad in Vrindavan.
Umakant and Ramakant Gundecha move to Bhopal to study with the Dagar brothers Zia Fariduddin and Zia Mohiuddin.
The Gundecha Brothers receive the Padma Shri.

future: Fund full-time gurukula places in dhrupad, since few students can afford years of voice training.
Support pakhawaj players and makers, who are fewer than singers.
Record alap and bandish from elders of the Dagar, Darbhanga and Bettiah families in full, with notes, and archive them openly.
Hold regular dhrupad concerts in Vrindavan, Gwalior and Darbhanga with fair fees.
Find and support women dhrupad singers, who have been few.
Give clear, simple listening guides for new audiences.

name: Ghazal
tagline: Couplets of longing, sung: a Persian form that became one of the voices of Urdu and Hindustani music.
facts: A ghazal is a poem of self-contained couplets (sher) with a refrain (radif) and rhyme (qafia)
The form came to South Asia around the 12th century and reached a peak in Urdu
Begum Akhtar was called Mallika-e-Ghazal (Queen of Ghazal)
Love poems can be read as human or divine love
art: A ghazal is a poem, and also a way of singing a poem. Wikipedia says it began in Arabic poetry in the 7th century, became central in Persian poetry, and spread across South Asia. It came to the subcontinent around the 12th century and was shaped here by poets such as Amir Khusrau.

The form has strict rules. A ghazal has five to fifteen couplets, each called a sher. Each couplet stands on its own, but all share a metre and a rhyme. The first couplet is the matla. The refrain that repeats at the end of each second line is the radif. The last couplet, the maqta, often has the poet's pen name. The subject is usually love and longing for a beloved who is out of reach. Because the beloved can be a person or God, many couplets can be read in both ways.

In music, the ghazal is sung in a light-classical way. The singer sets the words to a raga-based tune and stops to repeat and shade a line, so the audience hears the meaning of the couplet. A harmonium, tabla and sarangi or other string instrument usually accompany the singer.
In Urdu, the form reached a classical peak with poets such as Mir Taqi Mir and Mirza Ghalib, according to Wikipedia. Singers set their lines to music, and Ghalib's verses are still sung widely.
artist: Begum Akhtar (1914-1974), born Akhtaribai Faizabadi in Faizabad, is the singer most associated with the ghazal. She trained under several teachers, and the IGNCA timeline names Ata Mohammed Khan of the Patiala gharana and, later in Lucknow, Abdul Wahid Khan of the Kirana gharana. Her first HMV recording was in 1927. She married a Lucknow barrister in the early 1940s and largely stopped concerts, then returned to the stage in 1950. She is regarded as one of the greatest exponents of ghazal, dadra and thumri.

Her honours were the Padma Shri, the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for vocal music, and the Padma Bhushan, given after her death. Sources differ by a year on the dates, so we give none here. She died in Ahmedabad after her last concert, and is buried at Pasand Bagh in Lucknow, beside her mother.

Jagjit Singh (1941-2011), born in Sri Ganganagar in present-day Rajasthan, brought the ghazal to a wide audience with simpler arrangements and poetry chosen for ordinary listeners. He received the Padma Bhushan in 2003. Mehdi Hassan, who sang from Pakistan, is also named in sources on the form.
place: The ghazal does not belong to one place. Delhi and Lucknow were the great centres of Urdu poetry. Hyderabad under the Nizams was another, and Begum Akhtar received patronage there. Kolkata, with its recording houses, was where she made her first records.

Faizabad, now part of Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh, is her birthplace, and a Faizabad university has planned a memorial to her. In Lucknow her grave was restored in 2012, according to Wikipedia. Today the ghazal is sung in mehfils, in concerts and on recordings across India and beyond.

history.what: The ghazal takes shape in Arabic poetry from the qasida.
The form arrives in the Indian subcontinent through Persian.
Amir Khusrau helps blend it with local languages, according to Wikipedia.
Mir Taqi Mir and Mirza Ghalib bring Urdu ghazal to a peak.
Begum Akhtar makes her first HMV recording.
She returns to the stage in Delhi, billed as Begum Akhtar for the first time.
Jagjit Singh and Chitra Singh become widely known for light ghazal albums.
Begum Akhtar dies after her last concert in Ahmedabad.

future: Teach the poetry along with the singing, so young singers understand the couplets they perform.
Support accompanists such as sarangi and tabla players, whose numbers are falling.
Archive old radio and gramophone recordings of Begum Akhtar and others, with notes on lyrics and poets.
Pay poets and translators when their words are sung, and credit them on every recording.
Create small mehfil spaces in towns outside the big cities, where listeners can hear the form live.

name: Ghumot
tagline: A clay pot with a skin on its mouth, played at Ganesh puja and at the mando.
facts: Struck membranophone of Goa, a clay pot open at both ends
Declared a Goa state heritage instrument in August 2019
Skin was traditionally monitor lizard; now often goat skin
Played at Ganesh Chaturthi, Shigmo, Sao Joao and in the mando
art: The ghumot (also ghumat or gumot) is a clay pot drum. The larger opening is covered by a stretched hide. A smaller opening on the other side lets the player's hand control the air and tone. Wikipedia says the player uses both hands, one on the small opening and the other striking the skin.

The skin is soaked overnight, stretched over the mouth, bound with coir and banana fibre and dried in shade. Traditionally the hide was from the Indian monitor lizard. This lizard is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, so many makers now use goat skin or synthetic material.
The ghumot is usually played with the shamel (main rhythm drum) and kansallem (cymbals), a group called suvari vadan. A related drum, the mhadalem, has a skin at both ends.
artist: Potters make the earthen body, so the instrument depends on the Kumbhar community. Down To Earth reports that the number of makers is shrinking, and that some use lizard hide still, saying it sounds better. One potter recalled a police inquiry in 2018.

The same article asks whose heritage the label serves, pointing to caste hierarchy and the roles of soloists and accompanists. Wikipedia says local tribal communities are believed to have created the instrument and that classical musicians later formalised its use. The ghumata vazop dance was originally Kunbi, the article says, and has been adopted by others.
place: Among Hindus the ghumot is played at birth rituals (Satipujan), at Shigmo in Phalgun and at Ganesh Chaturthi prayers, including the aarti. Christians use it for pre-wedding roce, in the mando and dekhni, and at the Sao Joao festival on 24 June.
It is also played in parts of Karnataka and is known as gummeta in Andhra Pradesh, per Wikipedia.

history.what: Believed to have come with migrants and to have been made by a local tribal community. It is not named in classical Sanskrit treatises.
Monitor lizards were given legal protection, per Down To Earth.
Goa declared the ghumot a state heritage instrument. Down To Earth and Wikipedia agree on the date; they say the declaration is for ghumot made without lizard skin.

future: Support potters who make the pot bodies and pay fairly for them.
Develop and share good non-lizard skins, so tone does not suffer.
Offer lessons in school and village clubs.
Record the many rhythms across Hindu and Christian use.
Give players and accompanists recognition.

name: Gurbani Kirtan
tagline: Sacred verse set to raga, sung at the Golden Temple from before dawn into the night.
facts: Shabad kirtan began with Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana's rabab
Guru Arjan is said to have set five daily chaukis at Harmandir Sahib
Asa di Var is sung in the early morning
Hazoori ragis take rotating shifts
art: Shabad kirtan is the devotional singing of hymns from Sikh scripture. Inderjit N. Kaur writes that it is central to Sikh life and is a tradition of some five hundred years, beginning with Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539), who sang to the rabab of Bhai Mardana.

The Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga. Wikipedia counts 31 single ragas, with mixed ones bringing the total higher, and says scholars disagree about how the arrangement was set and what the ghar markings once meant.
Instruments include the rabab, saranda, taus, dilruba and jori. Wikipedia says the harmonium and tabla have largely replaced older instruments, and groups have shrunk from four performers to a trio.
Kaur proposes the term raga-based shabad kirtan for kirtan that uses raga, noting that the common term gurmat sangeet is relatively recent.
artist: Tradition holds that the descendants of Bhai Mardana became hereditary rababi musicians who served the later Gurus. Wikipedia says their tradition declined sharply after Partition in 1947, when many families moved to Pakistan.
The Golden Temple site says Hazoori ragis, appointed by the SGPC, perform in rotating two-hour shifts so kirtan does not stop, and visiting jathas perform on a schedule.
Ragis were traditionally trained in taksals such as Damdami Taksal, and newer institutions now teach Sikh music alone (Wikipedia).
place: Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is the centre of kirtan. Kaur says Guru Arjan is said to have started five chaukis (sittings) a day: Asa di Var at dawn, Anand mid-morning, Charan Kanwal at midday, Sodar in the evening and Kalyan at night.

The Golden Temple site says kirtan runs from the early hours until the Sukhasan ceremony at night and is relayed by speakers around the parikrama. The page gives both 'over 20 hours' and a timetable ending at 10 pm, so check the current times locally.

history.what: Sang his hymns with Mardana on the rabab, as the janam sakhis and later paintings show (Kaur).
Is said to have made Asa di Var a regular morning practice.
Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth, which includes saints of several faiths.
Is said to have started the five daily chaukis at Harmandir Sahib.
Wikipedia says persecution disrupted kirtan and Jassa Singh Ahluwalia helped revive it.
Sikh states such as Patiala, Nabha and Kapurthala patronised musicians (Wikipedia).
Partition ended the world of many rababi families.

future: Teach raga-based kirtan to children, with the older instruments, not only the harmonium.
Support revival of the rabab and its makers and players.
Offer stipends for young ragis in taksals and academies.
Record rare compositions and old styles with the senior ragis.
Keep clear, public notes on the daily schedule for visitors.

name: Gwalior Gharana
tagline: The oldest khayal gharana, rooted in a Tomar king's dhrupad school and a family of court singers.
facts: Form: Hindustani vocal music, khayal
Founders: Naththan Pir Bakhsh and grandsons Haddu and Hassu Khan
Style: straight taans, simple ragas
Court: Scindia patronage from 1810
art: The Gwalior gharana is a school of Hindustani classical singing, and Wikipedia calls it the first and most influential khayal gharana. It follows what the article calls the ashtangi gayaki, an eight-part framework: alap, behlava, taan, kampan, meend, gamaka, khatka and murki.

Wikipedia says it favours simplicity and well-known ragas. Its taans are straight (sapaat) rather than zig-zag, and it does not use an extra-slow alap. Vilambit khayals are sung relatively briskly. The article itself is flagged as needing more citations, so these descriptions are indicative.
Gwalior is also remembered for dhrupad. Sahapedia says Man Singh Tomar (reigned 1486 to 1516) founded a school of music at Gujari Mahal in Gwalior fort and helped write the treatise Mankutuhal.
artist: Sahapedia credits Ustad Naththan Pir Bux with the khayal style, and his grandsons Hassu and Haddu Khan and nephew Natthu Khan with refining it. Wikipedia gives Hassu Khan's death as 1859 and Haddu Khan's as 1875. Other sources give different dates, so these are not firm.

Pupils carried the style outward. Wikipedia says Balakrishnabuwa Ichalkaranjikar took it to Maharashtra, and Krishnarao Shankar Pandit trained his son Laxman Krishnarao Pandit and granddaughter Meeta Pandit. Sahapedia says he founded the Shankar Gandharva Vidyalaya in 1914.

Tansen is linked to Gwalior as a native of the area (Sahapedia) and a singer at Akbar's court. Sahapedia calls him a dhrupad composer. His link is to the older Gwalior dhrupad tradition, not to the khayal family above, as these sources present it.
place: Gwalior stands in northern Madhya Pradesh, with its fort above the city. Sahapedia says it became the Scindia capital in 1810, and that Daulatrao Scindia and Jayajirao Scindia supported musicians.
Tansen's tomb near the fort is still visited by locals, per Sahapedia. The city still has music schools that go back to the early twentieth century.

history.what: Man Singh Tomar rules and sets up a music school at Gwalior (Sahapedia).
Tansen, from near Gwalior, sings at Akbar's court.
Gwalior becomes the Scindia capital; court patronage grows.
Naththan Pir Bux is credited with the Gwalior khayal style under Daulatrao Scindia.
Hassu Khan and Haddu Khan die, as per Wikipedia; sources vary.
Gandharva Mahavidyalaya is founded by Vishnu Digambar Paluskar (1901) and Shankar Gandharva Vidyalaya by Krishnarao Shankar Pandit (1914).

future: Training: gurukul-style teaching in Gwalior, supported by schools such as Shankar Gandharva Vidyalaya.
Livelihood: concerts, radio and recordings that pay singers and accompanists.
Materials: keep the making of tanpuras and tablas alive in nearby workshops.
Documentation: record older singers and their compositions in the gharana.
Protection: archive recordings and notation so lesser-known bandishes are not lost.

name: Haryanvi Ragini
tagline: Sung story-poems of Haryana, made famous by Pandit Lakhmi Chand.
facts: Form: sung story-poem, also spelt raagni or ragni
Closely tied to Saang theatre
Linked to Pandit Lakhmi Chand (1903-1945)
Accompanied by instruments such as sarangi and harmonium
art: Ragini, also spelt raagni, is a folk song form of Haryana. It is sung stories, love, parting, devotion and moral teaching in Haryanvi verse. The Wikipedia page on the music of Haryana lists Ragini among the state's folk theatrical performances, alongside Rasa Lila.

The sources I read do not describe the metre or tune of a raagni in detail. What they do show is its close link to Saang. Wikipedia says singing in the raagni style is central to Saang, and the Tribune says Lakhmi Chand's raagnis were written on Vedanta, love and separation.

Instruments named for Haryanvi folk music in general include the sarangi, harmonium, dholak, dhadd and manjeera. The Tribune names a sarangi player, Dhoolia Khan, as Lakhmi Chand's teacher. Which instruments accompany a particular raagni can differ by troupe.
artist: Lakhmi Chand (1903-1945), called Suryakavi Pandit Lakhmi Chand and Dada Lakhmi Chand, was a Haryanvi poet. Wikipedia says he was born at Janti Kalan in Sonipat district to a farming family and had no formal schooling. It says the village's spelling varies. Wikipedia's music page says the Ragini form was popularised by him.

The Tribune says he composed raagni on the spot, trained for two decades with the sarangi player Dhoolia Khan, and wrote about 20 Saangs. Wikipedia lists 14 Saangs and names his disciples Mangeram Susana and Mehar Singh Barona. The two pages differ on his teachers and on the number of Saangs.

Wikipedia also lists Baje Bhagat, Bharatchandra Kaushik and Dayachand Mayna among early Haryanvi singers. Some honours and a film about Lakhmi Chand mentioned in Wikipedia lack citations, so they are left out here. I could not confirm any Sangeet Natak Akademi honour for him.
place: Raagni belongs to the villages and small towns of Haryana, especially Sonipat, Rohtak and Rewari districts, where the Saang poets lived. It is sung at fairs, weddings and gatherings, and in contests between singers.
Wikipedia notes that folk singers in Haryana are highly esteemed and invited to events regardless of caste or status.

history.what: Lakhmi Chand is born at Janti Kalan, Sonipat, according to Wikipedia.
He composes raagnis and Saangs in Haryanvi, and is named by the Tribune as the founder of the present raagni form.
Year of Lakhmi Chand's death, given in the lead of the Wikipedia article without a citation.
His son Tule Ram works to preserve his father's heritage, says the Tribune.
Haryanvi artists continue to perform his best-known work, Lakhmichand Ka Brahmgyaan, says Wikipedia.

future: Documentation: record elder singers and write out raagnis with the poet's name, so that authorship is not lost.
Training: create apprenticeships between older raagni singers and young singers.
Livelihood: support fair payment for festival and radio work, and care that popular recordings credit the original poets.
Scholarship: translate the major raagnis with notes on their poets.
Protection: archive recordings in public institutions.

name: Hindustani Music
tagline: A music of slow-unfolding ragas and rhythmic cycles, handed from teacher to student.
facts: Form: classical music of North India built on raga and tala
Taught through the guru-shishya (teacher-student) tradition
Styles passed down in families and schools called gharanas
Moved from courts to concert halls and radio in the 20th century
art: Hindustani music is the classical music of North India. It is built on two ideas. A raga is a melodic frame: a set of notes with its own rules, moods and characteristic phrases. A tala is a rhythmic cycle of a fixed number of beats. The musician does not read a score. Within the frame of the raga, he or she improvises, and the same raga is never sung twice in quite the same way.

A performance usually starts slowly, with the raga explored without a beat, and then settles into rhythm with a drum such as the tabla. A steady drone, played on the tanpura, sits underneath. Wikipedia notes that ragas are often grouped by their notes into parent scales called thaats, a system brought together around 1900 by Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande.

Several forms sit inside the tradition. Dhrupad is the older, austere form (see its own story). Khyal, meaning imagination, is the main concert form today and allows more ornament and free play. Lighter forms such as thumri and the devotional bhajan are also sung. Instruments include the sitar, sarod, bansuri flute, sarangi and santoor.

Ragas are linked to times of day and seasons. A morning raga is not meant to be sung at midnight. Listeners who do not know the rules can still follow: listen for the way a few notes are returned to again and again, and how the singer or player slowly builds the mood.
artist: Training has long been one to one. Until the late 19th century, Wikipedia says, a student learned from a single teacher, the guru or ustad, often living in the teacher's house. This had benefits, but students often spent much of their time serving the teacher, and the music stayed within a small community.

Musical styles were carried by families and schools called gharanas, many linked to princely courts. Wikipedia names Oudh, Patiala and Banaras among the court-linked schools, and the Gwalior school as important in the development of dhrupad. Other well-known gharana names are Agra, Kirana and Jaipur-Atrauli. I could not confirm in the sources I read which artists founded each school, so the founders are not named here. That needs a specialist source.

In the 20th century two teachers opened the art to wider groups. Vishnu Digambar Paluskar founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in 1901, a school open to all. Bhatkhande published the four-volume Hindustani Sangeeta Paddhati (1909 to 1932), which proposed a system of notation.
Accompanists matter too: tabla players, harmonium and sarangi players, and the instrument makers whose work is little recognised.
place: Hindustani music belongs to the north and centre of India, from Punjab in the west to Bengal in the east. Its homes are the old courts and cities: Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh, Agra, Lucknow and Banaras in Uttar Pradesh, Jaipur in Rajasthan, Patiala in Punjab, and Delhi.

Two court worlds shaped it. Under the Delhi Sultanate, Wikipedia says, rule brought wide cultural exchange, musicians came to courts, and Hindu and Muslim musical ideas mixed. Under the Mughals, Akbar's court patronised musicians such as Tansen, and rulers took interest in local forms. This exchange helped produce new forms such as khyal.

Music also lived in temples and shrines, in the singing of devotional poetry and in Sufi gatherings. After the 16th century, styles spread out into gharanas under different princely patrons. When royal patronage declined, government-run All India Radio helped bring artists to the public.

history.what: Ancient Sanskrit texts describe melodic and rhythmic theory. Scholars connect modern raga music to this long line but not directly.

Under the Delhi Sultanate, musicians moved into courts and Hindu and Muslim musical ideas mixed. Amir Khusrau (1253 to 1325) is traditionally credited with systematising parts of the music. Wikipedia says his link to the origin of khyal is not supported.
Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior is linked with the Mankutuhal, a work on the main forms of his time, and with dhrupad.
Under Akbar, the Mughal court patronised musicians such as Tansen. After this, singing styles split into gharanas under different courts.
Sadarang, a court musician under Muhammad Shah, may have been the father of modern khyal, says Wikipedia. The attribution is a scholar's view, not a certain fact.
Vishnu Digambar Paluskar founds the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya, a school open to all, moving training away from the closed gharana system.
Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande groups ragas into thaats and publishes Hindustani Sangeeta Paddhati (1909 to 1932).
Royal patronage declines. All India Radio and public concerts become the main stage for artists.

future: Support long-term teacher-student training with fair stipends for gurus, so the one-to-one tradition survives alongside classroom teaching.
Give accompanists and instrument makers (tabla, sitar, sarangi) recognition, training places and fair pay.
Record elders in full, with notes on raga, bandish and teacher lineage, and keep the recordings in open archives.
Offer free or low-cost concerts and listening introductions in small towns, so the music reaches new audiences.
Work with gharana families to document their repertoire before it is lost, and let the families decide what is made public.
Teach the basics of raga and tala in schools, in Hindi and local languages.
