name: Kumaoni Holi
tagline: Holi in the Kumaon hills is sung for weeks, seated in raga, then standing in the open.
facts: Forms: Baithaki, Khari (Khadi) and Mahila Holi
Songs based on classical ragas, with Kumaoni folk influence
Begins in winter and runs almost two months
Traditionally traced to the Chand court at Champawat, 15th century
art: Kumaoni Holi is a musical festival. Wikipedia and Outlook Traveller describe three main forms. Baithaki Holi is sung seated, in homes and temple courtyards. Khari (Khadi) Holi is sung and danced standing, mostly in villages. Mahila Holi is sung by women.

Baithaki songs follow classical ragas. DailyO lists Peelu, Bhimpalasi and Sarang for noon sittings, and Kalyan, Shyam Kalyan and Yaman for the evening. Harmonium and tabla are central. Songs are in Hindi, Braj bhasha and Kumaoni.
The mood changes through the season. The first phase, called Nirvan ki Holi, has devotional songs. After Basant Panchami the themes turn to love and beauty, with many songs on Radha and Krishna.
Khari Holi groups, called tolis, visit houses singing blessings for the household. Dancers wear white kurtas, churidar pyjamas and pointed caps, and move to dhol and hurka drum.
Cheer Bandhan and Cheer Dahan are the ritual tying and burning of the cheer, the festival's centre, before the colour day.
artist: The singers are called Holiyars. The sources I read do not list names of notable ones, except that Wikipedia mentions a Champawat singer, Heera Ballabh Bhatt, as well known.

DailyO says a family that hosts a Baithaki sitting is expected to host it every year, and to invite everyone to the next sitting. Singers are given tea and machwani, a warm milk drink with ginger and black pepper.
Kumaonis living in other cities also keep up all three forms.
place: Kumaoni Holi belongs to Kumaon, the eastern hills of Uttarakhand. The sources link its musical form to Champawat, where the Chand kings held court. Wikipedia and a web search also found a claim that Almora, the later Chand capital, was the origin, so the place of origin is not settled.
Today Baithaki Holi is heard in Almora, Pithoragarh, Champawat and other towns, and Khari Holi in the villages. Songs begin at Basant Panchami and some areas start as early as Paush in December.

history.what: Outlook Traveller and DailyO trace the tradition to the court of the Chand kings in Champawat, where Braj musical styles met Kumaoni ones. Sources repeat this date and I found no independent documentation.
As the Chand kingdom grew, Holi singing spread across Kumaon and took on a local character.
Wikipedia cites E. T. Atkinson's Himalayan Gazetteer and B. D. Pandey's History of Kumaun as background reading. I did not read these books.
The festival is now a draw for visitors and for Kumaonis returning home.

future: Training: hold sittings where older Holiyars teach ragas and lyrics to young singers, boys and girls.
Livelihood: pay singers and instrument players for performances outside the festival season.
Materials: keep tabla, harmonium and drum makers and repairers in the hill towns.
Documentation: record the songs in their ragas and in Kumaoni, with the names of the singers.
Protection: keep Mahila Holi and village Khari Holi visible, not only the town sittings.

name: Mando and Dekhni
tagline: Songs of love, loss and local news, from the Catholic houses of Salcete.
facts: Mando: Goan Catholic dance song, mainly 19th-20th century
Played with violin, guitar and ghumot
Dekhni: a related dance song with Hindu themes
Classical mandos use the Salcete dialect of Konkani
art: The mando is a Goan song and dance of the Catholic community. Wikipedia describes it as a form that grew in the 19th and 20th centuries and blended Goan and Western traditions. Most mandos come from villages of Salcete. It is usually sung in the first person, and love is the main theme. The singers sway gently to the rhythm. It is accompanied by guitar, violin and the ghumot drum.

Dr Alvarinho Luis, writing in The Goan, lists four themes: longing for a lover, lament over loss, union, and the telling of local or political events. Because there was little mass media, some mandos worked as public comment. He names 'Luizinha Mhojea Luizinha', based on the 1854 murder of a Portuguese captain at Divar, and a fast section recalling a shooting at Holy Spirit Church in Margao in 1880.

The dekhni is a dance song of Goan Christians, close to the mando but with Hindu themes. Panjim.org says it is sung in two voices, usually with shehnai, tabla and cymbals, and was danced after the mando at big gatherings. One reading of it, given on that page, is that it expresses nostalgia for a Hindu past, while the mando shows acceptance of Christianity. A Gomantak Times piece describes the dekhni as a women's dance with ghumot and small clay lamps; its best known song is 'Hanv Saiba Poltoddi Vetam'. Sources differ on whether it is mainly a song or a dance.
artist: Mando was once kept to elite Brahmin families of Salcete and their homes, according to Dr Luis. It later spread across Goan society and is now sung at roce ceremonies, weddings and gatherings.

Composers named in the same article are Dr Jose Inacio de Loyola, who wrote a mando on the 1880 Margao events, and Paulo Milagres Silva (1855-1931) and Arnaldo de Menezes (1863-1917), whose songs a Portuguese governor is said to have seen danced in 1877-78. The Department of Art and Culture and Kala Academy hold annual mando competitions.
Traditionally the dancers wore velvet or silk embroidered with gold thread and used a fan, per Wikipedia.
place: Mando belongs to the villages of Salcete in South Goa. Dr Luis names Curtorim, Loutolim and Raia for early work, and Margao was a centre of the community.
Many Portuguese words appear in mandos, which suggests the form grew during Portuguese rule.

history.what: Panjim.org says the mando grew out of the ovi, a nuptial song form used in church hymns, and likely gained its refrain around 1840 under the influence of Portuguese fado.
The first mando is reportedly written and sung at Curtorim, according to The Goan. The scholar Filipe Neri Xavier dated it to 1846 among Salcete Brahmins. Dates differ.
'Luizinha Mhojea Luizinha' is said to be based on a murder at Divar in this year.
A shooting of civilians at Holy Spirit Church, Margao, during a municipal election, remembered in a mando.
Mando competitions by the Department of Art and Culture and Kala Academy help spread the form beyond the old elite.

future: Keep the classical Salcete dialect alive by recording old mandos with singers and meanings.
Teach the dance and its dress to young people in schools and cultural clubs.
Pay violin, guitar and ghumot players for performances.
Archive old manuscripts and family collections of mandos.
Support the annual competitions and open them to singers from all communities.

name: Manganiyar and Langa Music
tagline: Desert songs carried by hereditary Muslim musicians for their Hindu patrons.
facts: Region: Jaisalmer and Barmer in the Thar Desert
Hereditary Muslim musicians with Hindu patrons (jajman)
Instruments: kamaicha, khartal (kartaal), dholak
Songs are called oral history of the desert
art: The Manganiyar (also spelt Manganiar) are a community of hereditary professional musicians in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan, mainly in Barmer and Jaisalmer. Their songs speak of people, nature and salvation. The Hindu newspaper calls them oral historians of the desert, because the songs carry local memory from one generation to the next.

The kamaicha is a bowed instrument with 17 strings and is related to the sarangi, Wikipedia says. The kartaal (khartal) is a pair of teak pieces clapped like castanets. The dholak is a hand drum. Wikipedia adds that some of their ragas began in the Thar and are not found in North Indian classical music.

The Langa are a related community of musicians in the same region. I could not find a full source on the Langa in this research, so details of their instruments and songs are left out and should be added with a proper source.
Songs are sung at births, weddings and other family events, in the homes of their patrons.
artist: Wikipedia describes the Manganiyar as a Muslim community of hereditary musicians. Their traditional patrons, called jajman, are the locally dominant Hindu Rajput and Charan communities, who supported their music for generations. This jajmani relationship tied each musician family to patron families.
The name is linked to the words for begging (mangan) and garland (har), and a legend ties it to a gift of a necklace from Bibi Fatema. This is a legend, not a historic fact.
Named musicians in Wikipedia include Sakar Khan, a kamaicha player and Padma Shri recipient, and Lakha Khan, a singer and sarangi player.
Children learn by sitting with elders and playing from a very young age. Related communities live across the border in Sindh, Pakistan.
place: The Thar Desert covers western Rajasthan. Jaisalmer and Barmer, near the border with Pakistan, are dry, sparsely settled lands where distances are great and music was one of the few arts that could travel.

Patrons were Rajput and Charan families, and the Rajput forts and homes were stages for songs of lineage and heroism. Mehrangarh Fort in Jodhpur today hosts the Rajasthan International Folk Festival, founded in October 2007 by the Mehrangarh Museum Trust and the Jaipur Virasat Foundation and timed to Sharad Purnima. Wikipedia says the 2013 edition included sessions on the culture of the Manganiar of Marwar.
I could not verify the role of the Jaisalmer Desert Festival or the Rajasthan Roots project in these sources, so they are not described here.

history.what: Oral accounts link the Manganiyar to Rajput courts, but I could not find a firm date for the start of the jajmani relationship.
Songs and instruments are passed down within families as desert oral history, Wikipedia says.
The old system of patronage weakens as courts and landed patrons lose influence. A source for the exact process is needed.
Rajasthan International Folk Festival is founded at Mehrangarh, Jodhpur.
The festival holds sessions on the culture of the Manganiar of Marwar.

future: Support children of musician families with schooling, so they can learn music and also have other options.
Pay fair fees for festival and private concerts, with written agreements that name the musicians.
Record elders and make kamaicha makers' work visible, with local-language notes.
Document the Langa repertoire with community members as the main voices.
Fund a village music school in Barmer and Jaisalmer run by hereditary musicians.
Protect songs and rights so that recordings and fusion projects share income with the families.

name: Miraj Sitar and Tanpura Making
tagline: In one lane of a Krishna valley town, families have shaped sitars and tanpuras by hand for about 150 years.
facts: Place: Sitarmaker Galli, Miraj (renamed Faridsaheb Sitarmaker Marg)
GI: sitars and tanpuras of Miraj, granted 30 March 2024
Gourds: grown in Solapur district, near Pandharpur
Makers: more than 450 craftspeople in the cluster, by their own count
art: The sitar and the tanpura are central to Hindustani classical music. The tanpura gives the steady drone that a singer or sitar player tunes against. At Miraj both are built by hand, mostly with little power machinery, in small family workshops.

A sitar has a large resonator made from a seasoned gourd (tumba), a long wooden neck and a tabli, a thin wooden face. The gourd is the key material. A Sahapedia article says the founder, Faridsaheb, noticed that sadhus carried gourds as water pots (kamandalu) and saw that gourds could be good resonators for the sitar, veena and tanpura.

The same article credits Faridsaheb with refining the javari, the bridge detail that gives the strings their ringing tone. It says each sitar is tailored to the player. Pandit Ravi Shankar and Ustad Vilayat Khan had instruments made in Miraj, and some sitar styles carry their names.

In March 2024 the Indian GI registry gave two tags: one to the Miraj Musical Instruments Cluster for sitars, and one to a firm called Soultune Musical Instrument Producer for tanpuras. The makers had applied in 2021 after complaints that instruments from elsewhere were sold as Miraj-made. This is as reported by PTI in The Week.
artist: Sahapedia tells of the Shikalgar community, metalsmiths who repaired arms. It says they arrived in Miraj under the Adil Shahis in the 17th century. When firearms replaced older weapons, demand fell and the community turned to carpentry and then to musical instruments. The makers' own account in The Week is similar.

Faridsaheb (1827 to 1898) is named by Sahapedia as the founder of the local instrument craft. It says his brother Moinuddin helped with trials, and that the craft passed to his son Abdul Ghani and grandson Hussainsaheb. Another version in The Week says two brothers named Farid Mohideen Saheb Shikalgar and Farid Saheb Shikalgar impressed a visiting singer by repairing his tanpura about 200 years ago. Accounts differ on names and dates, so treat them as family and local tradition.

The makers describe seven generations of work. The Week quotes Mohsin Mirajkar, chairman of the cluster, as a descendant of these workers. Knowledge passes in families through hands-on practice rather than books.
The GI report says the cluster has more than 450 craftsmen who together make about 60 to 70 sitars and about 100 tanpuras a month. These figures are the makers' own claims.
place: Miraj is in Sangli district in southern Maharashtra, on the Krishna river plain. It was the seat of a small princely state under the Patwardhan family. Sahapedia says the rulers supported musicians, and Balasaheb Patwardhan II invited performers from across the subcontinent, making Miraj a centre of Hindustani music that influenced the Kirana gharana.

The gourds are the town's most unusual material. The Week says pumpkin gourds come from the Mangalvedha area of Solapur district and that gourd farming was encouraged along the Krishna river. Other reports say bitter gourds grown near Pandharpur, about 130 km away, are used. The wood for necks and faces comes from forests in Karnataka according to The Week.

The making lane is Sitarmaker Galli, now officially Faridsaheb Sitarmaker Marg. The town is also known for Sufi shrines and a long history of classical music, and musicians came here to have instruments repaired and built. That mix of craft and a musical court is why the trade settled here.

history.what: The Shikalgar community, who repaired arms, are said to arrive in Miraj under the Adil Shahis.
Maratha rule follows; in 1820 the town is split into two jagirs, according to Sahapedia.

Firearms replace older weapons; the Shikalgar community takes up carpentry and then instrument making. The Week places a tanpura repair about 200 years ago, with the Patwardhan ruler then encouraging the trade.
The life span given for Faridsaheb, the founding figure.
Pandit Ravi Shankar and Ustad Vilayat Khan have instruments made in Miraj, per Sahapedia.
Makers apply for a GI tag after other places sold instruments as Miraj-made.
GI tags are issued for Miraj sitars and tanpuras.

future: Train young makers through paid apprenticeships with master families, covering gourd selection, carving and tuning.
Support gourd farmers along the Krishna and in Solapur with seed, drying yards and assured purchase.
Secure legal wood supply from managed sources, and plan for scarcity of old seasoned timber.
Use the GI to stop copies, with a simple maker registry and a mark that tells buyers an instrument is truly from Miraj.
Document each stage on film and write down tonal rules (javari, tabli thickness) with the makers' approval.
Give instrument makers a name beside the players, with maker's names on instruments and at concerts.

name: Mridangam Making
tagline: A drum of jackfruit wood and layered hide, tuned by hand, made by communities who rarely get the credit.
facts: Body: hollowed jackfruit wood
Heads: goat, cow or buffalo skin, in layers
Black paste on the small head: rice flour, iron oxide, starch
Makers: Dalit Christian families in Chennai, Kollan families in Peruvemba
art: The mridangam is the main drum of Carnatic music. It has two heads of different size, so one drum gives both bass and treble. Wikipedia says the body is traditionally hollowed from jackfruit wood and the heads are goat, cow or buffalo skin, laced together with leather straps that are tightened to tune the drum.

The smaller head carries a black circle of paste, a mix of rice flour, iron oxide and starch, which gives the metallic ring. Wikipedia names it saatham or karanai; other writers use the word soru. The paste gives the drum its sound and must be right for the pitch. Before play, a paste of semolina is put on the bass head to deepen it, Wikipedia adds.

Skins are layered, but sources describe the layers differently. A Palakkad report in The News Minute says a cow skin is supported by a buffalo skin, with straps to tighten the cover. A Chennai report says the head has a thick outer ring, a middle layer and a top layer of goat skin. Treat the exact layers as differing by workshop.

Raw hides must be washed, stretched, pegged and sun-dried for weeks before use. The Palakkad makers told The News Minute that rain slows drying and affects tone, and that cattle fed on cattle feed give fattier skin which is harder to tan.

A Chennai maker quoted in the Mylapore reports works on several drums at once and takes about seven days for each. The skill is in the ear: the maker hears the pitch and adjusts the skin and paste until the drum sings.
artist: In Chennai, the best-known makers work in Mylapore. Reports say they came from Thanjavur. Several sources describe them as Dalit and often Dalit Christian, and one Outlook piece traces their ancestry to the Paraiyar community. Their forebears hoped conversion would end untouchability, but the piece says it did not. One family is reported to trace its work back to the time of the composer Thyagaraja (1767 to 1847).

Working with raw cowhide has long been treated as unclean by caste custom, and sources say that brought stigma to the makers even as their drums were used in temples and concert halls. T. M. Krishna's book Sebastian and Sons: A Brief History of Mrdangam Makers (2020) tells this story through a Thanjavur family. It is the best-known treatment of the subject, and I have not read it in full.

In Kerala, craftsmen of the Kollan community in Peruvemba village, about 15 km from Palakkad, have made drums for over two centuries, according to The News Minute. In 2007 about 60 craftsmen from several families formed a cooperative, the Thukal Vadyopakarna Nirmana Sangam. NABARD and Vision India Charitable Trust support a cluster project there.

Makers in both places report low earnings, little government support and an uncertain supply of good hide. The Palakkad craftsmen asked for pensions and said they get none. I did not find named makers in the sources apart from families and cooperatives mentioned here, and I have chosen not to name individuals I could not check.
place: Mridangam making is spread between two places. In Tamil Nadu, Thanjavur and Chennai (Mylapore) are the main centres, where musicians come to buy and repair. In Kerala, Peruvemba near Palakkad makes mridangams, maddalams and other drums.

The materials come from the surrounding country. Jackfruit trees grow in the wet south, and the log is dried before it is hollowed. Hides come from abattoirs. The Mylapore makers buy cowhide from Thanjavur and Ambur, and the Palakkad makers also buy from abattoirs. Rice and other items for the paste are from the local market.

The drum belongs to temple and concert life alike. Wikipedia notes that Tamil Sangam literature mentions a drum called tannumai, and that the Silappadikaram describes drum ensembles in dramatic performance. These are old references to drums in general, and scholars debate how far they describe the modern mridangam. In Kerala, the Mridangamela is held at the Koodalmanikyam temple, Irinjalakuda.

history.what: Sangam-era Tamil texts and the Silappadikaram mention drums that later writers connect to the mridangam. The name is from Sanskrit words for clay and limb, which suggests early clay bodies; wood replaced clay later.
The mridangam becomes the main percussion instrument of Carnatic music along with the growth of the tala system.
The Kollan families of Peruvemba are said to have been making drums for over two centuries.
One Chennai family traces its drum-making back to this time, by its own account.
Makers move from Thanjavur to Mylapore, Chennai, near the concert world.
About 60 Peruvemba craftsmen form a cooperative.
T. M. Krishna publishes Sebastian and Sons, a history of mridangam makers.

future: Treat makers as artists: credit them on programmes, in the music season and in awards, and record their stories in their own words.
Pay a fair price and offer pensions and health cover through cooperatives like the one in Peruvemba.
Secure legal, clean hide supply, with training in safe tanning, and look at new ways to dry skins in the monsoon.
Set up apprenticeships for young people from the maker families, with a recognised certificate and a path to open workshops.
Record each step of making, including the paste, on film with the makers, and keep copies with them.
Work with musicians and music sabhas to end stigma and hold public events in the makers' neighbourhoods.

name: Nadaswaram and Thavil
tagline: A loud, bright reed pipe and a two-headed drum, the sound of an auspicious day.
facts: Nadaswaram: double-reed pipe, traditionally of aacha wood
Thavil: barrel drum of jackfruit wood, played with a stick and thumb caps
Narasingapettai nagaswaram: GI-tagged in March 2022
Played as mangala vadyam, auspicious music
art: The nadaswaram is a double-reed instrument with a conical bore that widens to a metal bell. Wikipedia says it has seven finger-holes and five lower holes that can be stopped with wax. The reed, seevali, is made of dried grass. It is loud, so it suits open air, temples and processions. It is played at almost all Hindu weddings and temple events in the South Indian tradition.

The thavil is a cylinder hollowed from one block of jackfruit wood, with skin on both ends held by hemp hoops. Wikipedia says the right head is played with the hand, with thumb caps made of hardened flour glue, and the left head with a short stick. It usually accompanies the nadaswaram.

PARI describes making the nadaswaram. A cylindrical block of wood is turned on a lathe, once hand-turned and now sometimes motor-driven. Cutting, filing and drilling need exact work, and each instrument takes about three people. The flared lower end, the anusu, is fitted at the end.
The instrument is called a mangala vadyam, an auspicious instrument. N. R. Selvaraj of Narasingapettai told PARI it originated in this area, near Mayavaram.
artist: PARI names four families still making nadaswarams in Narasingapettai, among them N. R. Selvaraj, a fourth-generation maker, his uncle Sakthivel Achari and Sakthivel's son Senthilkumar. Selvaraj's great-grandfather, Govindasamy Achari, learned the craft near Mayavaram and brought it to the village.

Selvaraj's father, Ranganathan Achari, is credited with a 1955 redesign that lets all seven swaras sound. PARI says makers earn about Rs 1,000 profit per instrument, and some younger family members are choosing other careers.
Wikipedia lists master nadaswaram players such as T. N. Rajarathnam Pillai and Karukurichi Arunachalam, and thavil players such as Thirumulaivayil Muthuveer Pillai and Valayapatti A. R. Subramaniam.
place: The nadaswaram and the thavil are played together at temples, weddings and festivals across Tamil Nadu. Wikipedia links the thavil to Thanjavur and says most thavils are made in Thanjavur and Valayapatti.

Narasingapettai is a village near Kumbakonam where a few families still make the nadaswaram by hand. PARI places it in Nagapattinam district, while news reports on the GI tag place it in Thanjavur district, so sources differ.

Many makers say the wood is a problem. PARI reports that the aacha wood must be 75 to 100 years old, so makers reuse old lintels and pillars, and they are sometimes stopped at check posts on suspicion of carrying sandalwood.

history.what: Wikipedia says the instrument appears, spelled nagaswaram, in Vijayanagara-era land grant inscriptions from the mid-1400s and in inscriptions of Achyuta Deva Raya from around the 1530s.
A treatise called Padasangraham mentions it (Wikipedia).
Ranganathan Achari of Narasingapettai is credited with the redesign that made all seven swaras sound (PARI).
An application for a Geographical Indication was filed by the Thanjavur Musical Instruments Workers Co-operative Cottage Industrial Society (Gulf News).
The Narasinghapettai nagaswaram received a GI tag. Reports differ on the certificate number, so check the GI registry.

future: Secure a legal supply of seasoned aacha wood, and plant trees for the makers of the future.
Help makers get fair prices, and use the GI tag to protect them from imitations.
Fund apprenticeships for young makers, and for young nadaswaram and thavil players.
Record the making process and the playing styles of senior players, with the makers' own words.
Look at new materials for the body of the instrument, in talks with players, so that the sound is not lost.

name: Nata Sankirtana
tagline: Drummers and singer-dancers tell the life of Krishna in the round, on UNESCO's list since 2013.
facts: Part of Sankirtana, inscribed by UNESCO in 2013
Typically two drummers and about ten singer-dancers
Performed in the round in a temple hall (mandapa)
Practised by the Vaishnava communities of the Manipur plains
art: Sankirtana is a group of arts performed on religious occasions and at key stages of life among the Vaishnava people of Manipur's plains. Singers, drummers and dancers tell the stories of Krishna. UNESCO describes a typical performance as two drummers and about ten singer-dancers, with devotees seated around them.

Nata Pala is the main temple repertoire, performed across the Manipur valley, according to Wikipedia. Other forms it names are Ariba Pala and Manohar Sai Pala (less common today), seasonal forms such as Holi Pala, Shayan and Khubak Eshei, and domestic Sankirtana at ceremonies such as ear-piercing, the sacred thread, marriage and death rites.

The setting matters. Performances are given in the round in a temple hall, or sometimes in a home courtyard. UNESCO says the energy can be so strong that audience members are moved to tears or bow before the performers.
artist: UNESCO says the knowledge and skills are passed from mentor to disciple. The performers are community members, and the devotees who sit around the performers take part as well as watch.
We did not find a source we could read that names individual living performers, so this entry does not name any.
place: Sankirtana is centred on the temple, and the Manipur valley around Imphal is its main home. Wikipedia says it is practised mainly by Meitei Hindus, who are mostly Vaishnavas, and by Vaishnava Manipuri communities in Tripura and Assam.
UNESCO says the practice brings people together during festivals through the year and connects individuals to the community through life-cycle ceremonies.

history.what: Wikipedia says the art draws on Manipur's pre-Vaishnavite past.
Wikipedia gives the era of origin as the 18th century to the present. Sources differ on exact dates and on who shaped the form, so this entry does not give a founder.
UNESCO inscribed Sankirtana, ritual singing, drumming and dancing of Manipur on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (nomination file 00843, submitted by India).
UNESCO notes the practice is listed in India's national inventory kept by the Sangeet Natak Akademi.

future: Training: support mentor-to-disciple teaching, with young drummers and singers learning in temple halls and schools.
Livelihood: pay performers and teachers for festivals and cultural programmes, and keep their ritual role distinct from stage shows.
Documentation: record the repertoires (Nata Pala and the others) with the community's consent, in audio, video and written notation.
Protection: keep the practice in its home setting, since UNESCO ties it to temple and life-cycle occasions.
Access: when presenting it to outsiders, explain the context before the performance.

name: Pena Music
tagline: A one-string bowed fiddle of coconut shell and bamboo, played to wake and lull the gods.
facts: Single-string bowed lute of the Meitei
Body of bamboo tube fixed to half a coconut shell
Used mainly in Lai Haraoba
Wikipedia reports only 145 active players
art: The pena is a single-string bowed instrument of the Meitei people. Wikipedia describes the body as a bamboo tube about 10 to 11 inches long fixed to half a coconut shell, with two sound holes, one covered with dried animal skin. A bamboo peg sets the string tension. The bow is wooden with a curved metal end, and the string is traditionally horsehair.

In Lai Haraoba the pena has a clear role. Sahapedia says a pena player awakens the deity at dawn each day and ends the first day with a lullaby. One dance, the laiching jagoi, is done with the fiddle alone, without song.
Wikipedia calls it one of the oldest Meitei instruments and says it was also played at royal gatherings.
artist: The player is called the pena asheiba. Wikipedia names several players, among them Khangembam Mangi Singh, Guru N. G. Ibopishak, Leimapokpam Yaima and Mayanglambam Mangangsana.

Khangembam Mangi Singh (1927-2022), known as Guru Pena Mangi, was born in Lambal, Imphal, and learned from his father and other teachers. He played for King Budhachandra, taught at the Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy from 1975 to 1996, and was a founding member of Laihui, a research centre for traditional performing arts begun in 1985. He received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 2006 and the Padma Shri in 2011, the first pena player to do so.
Sahapedia notes that the asheiba tradition is open only to men.
place: The pena belongs to the Meitei world of the Manipur valley and to the shrines where Lai Haraoba is held. Mangi Singh was from Lambal in Imphal, and the Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy in Imphal is where he taught.

history.what: Wikipedia describes the pena as one of the oldest Meitei instruments. No firm date is given.
It was played at royal gatherings, according to Wikipedia, and Mangi Singh is said to have performed for King Budhachandra.
Mangi Singh taught at the Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy.
Laihui, a research centre for traditional performing arts, was founded; Mangi Singh was a founding member.
Mangi Singh received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award and then the Padma Shri.

future: Training: more teachers and students, since Wikipedia reports only 145 active players, a figure that comes from a single source.
Livelihood: steady work for players at shrines and in cultural programmes.
Materials: support makers who build the pena from bamboo, coconut shell and horsehair.
Documentation: record the repertoire and the Lai Haraoba songs, building on the work of Laihui.
Protection: keep the pena tied to the ritual that gives it meaning.

name: Powada
tagline: A ballad sung to glorify, then bent to challenge power.
facts: Form: Marathi ballad, composed and sung by shahirs
The word powada means to glorify
Traditionally the earliest, Afzal Khanacha Vadh, is dated to 1659
Used by Phule, Annabhau Sathe and Amar Sheikh for reform and protest
art: A powada is a Marathi ballad. Wikipedia says the word means to glorify. Powadas first celebrated heroes and battles, and the oldest well-known one, Afzal Khanacha Vadh, tells of the clash between Shivaji and Afzal Khan. Forward Press attributes it to Agnidas and dates it to 1659, while other sources spell the poet's name differently.

The singer-composer is called a shahir. Janata Weekly says performances were largely improvised and that shahirs rarely worked from written texts. The ballad moves between sections with changes of rhythm called chaal.

The same form has been used for very different aims. Forward Press says powadas were later used in the national movement and in people's movements. Janata Weekly says Jyotirao Phule was probably the first to use the powada as satire against Brahmin dominance.
artist: Wikipedia, Janata Weekly and Forward Press all say powada was first sung by the Gondhali community, a Dalit community in their words. After Shivaji, Forward Press says, people of all castes took it up.

The sources name many shahirs. Forward Press lists Agnidas, Tulsidas (who wrote on Sinhagad), and in the Peshwa era Ramjoshi, Ananphandi, Honaji Bala and Prabhakar. Phule wrote powadas in the 19th century, including one on Shivaji. In the 1950s Amar Sheikh and Annabhau Sathe sang powadas in the Samyukta Maharashtra movement. Sambhaji Bhagat is named as a leading present-day shahir.
Harry Acworth and Shankar Tukaram Shaligram published about 60 powadas in 1891, per Forward Press. Our approach: name the shahirs and keep them central.
place: Powada belongs to Maharashtra as a whole, and is heard at fairs, rallies and public gatherings. Its early heroes are linked with forts such as Sinhagad, and its later rallies with the cities and workers of the Samyukta Maharashtra period.
It also travels. Wikipedia notes that the genre is popular in Kumaon and Garhwal in Uttarakhand, where it is called bhada. We have not examined that link and mention it for completeness.

history.what: Afzal Khanacha Vadh is described as the first powada by Forward Press and a Maharashtra gazette cited by Janata Weekly.
Forward Press calls the Shivaji era (1630 to 1680) the golden age of powada.
Janata Weekly names Ram Joshi, Anant Phandi and Honaji Bala as shahirs.
Jotirao Phule writes powadas, including on Shivaji and on Brahman Pantoji in the school department.
About 60 powadas are published by Acworth and Shaligram.
Amar Sheikh and Annabhau Sathe use powada in the Samyukta Maharashtra movement.
Janata Weekly says Ambedkarite and left groups used powada for protest.

future: Training: schools of shahirs and young singers under senior masters.
Livelihood: fees for shahirs at public events and on stage.
Materials: archives of recordings, and instruments for young performers.
Documentation: record oral powadas and share them with the singers' permission.
Protection: credit composers and communities, and keep alive both the heroic and reform strands.

name: Qawwali
tagline: Sufi devotional singing: call and response, building to ecstasy.
facts: Form: Sufi devotional music of South Asia
Sung at dargahs, especially on Urs (death anniversaries)
Amir Khusrau is traditionally credited with developing it
Nizamuddin Dargah holds qawwali every Thursday night
art: Qawwali is Sufi Islamic devotional music from South Asia. Wikipedia describes its purpose as remembering God (dhikr), bringing about spiritual ecstasy (wajd), and drawing listeners closer to God. The word comes from the Arabic qawl, meaning saying or utterance.

A qawwali is sung by a group, typically eight or nine men. They include lead and side singers, harmonium players, percussionists and a chorus that claps and repeats lines. This is call and response: the lead singer sings a line and the chorus answers.

Performances start quietly, with an instrumental prelude and an alap without rhythm, then verses, and then the main song with percussion and clapping. The energy rises through repetition and often ends abruptly. Singers may add sargam (sung note names) or improvise.

Early sources show qawwali was sung without instruments, and that the sarangi came before the harmonium. Today the harmonium, tabla and dholak are common. Songs are in Persian, Hindavi, Urdu and Punjabi.
artist: Qawwali is carried by families of professional singers called qawwals, who learn by singing with elders. I could not find a source in this research for named Delhi qawwal families, so they are not listed here.

Amir Khusrau (1253 to 1325) is widely credited with developing qawwali. Wikipedia says this is a tradition rather than a firmly documented fact. Likewise, Khusrau's authorship of specific works such as Man Kunto Maula is described as traditionally associated, not confirmed.

In the late 20th century, Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, Aziz Mian and the Sabri Brothers brought qawwali to a world audience, with Real World Records and WOMAD helping. These artists are from Pakistan, and are mentioned for the global history of the form.
Singers are trained from childhood, and the quality of a qawwali is judged by how it moves those listening, not only by technique.
place: Qawwali is sung at Sufi shrines, called dargahs, especially for the Urs, the saint's death anniversary. Two great Indian shrines are in Delhi and Ajmer.

The Nizamuddin Dargah is in Nizamuddin West, Delhi. Amir Khusrau was a disciple of the Chishti saint Nizamuddin Auliya, and the gatherings for listening (mehfil-e-sama) were held in the saint's khanqah. Khusrau's tomb stands at the entrance to the complex. The dargah holds a qawwali session every Thursday night, which draws about 1,500 visitors, and regular qawwali every evening after the Maghrib prayer.
Ajmer Sharif Dargah in Rajasthan also hosts qawwali, but the sources I read gave no detail about its history of music, so more research is needed.

history.what: Amir Khusrau, a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, is traditionally credited with developing qawwali. Gatherings called mehfil-e-sama were held at the saint's khanqah in Delhi.
The main tomb at Nizamuddin is built after the saint's death. Khusrau also died around this time (his dates are 1253 to 1325 per Wikipedia).
Qawwali spreads to shrines across South Asia, including Ajmer. Exact dates are not confirmed in the sources I read.
Early sources show it was sung a cappella or with the sarangi. The harmonium later became preferred.
Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, Aziz Mian and the Sabri Brothers bring qawwali to a global audience.
Nizamuddin Dargah holds qawwali each evening after Maghrib and every Thursday night.

future: Support qawwal families with regular fees and training for the next generation.
Record shrine qawwali, with full texts and translations from Persian, Hindavi and Urdu.
Let visitors learn the etiquette of listening at a dargah before concerts.
Keep shrine qawwali free and open to all who come, while ensuring that qawwals are fairly paid.
Protect heritage songs and credits when recordings are reused in film and pop.
Hold qawwali workshops in schools and music colleges.

name: Rabindra Sangeet
tagline: More than two thousand songs by one poet, where words and tune are given equal weight.
facts: About 2,232 songs, collected in the Gitabitan
Sections: Puja, Prem, Prakriti, Swadesh, Anusthanik, Vichitra
Name introduced by Dhurjati Prasad Mukherjee in 1931
Visva-Bharati publishes the Gitabitan volumes
art: Rabindra Sangeet means the songs of Rabindranath Tagore. He wrote and tuned about 2,232 of them over some 68 years, up to his last birthday in 1941. They are gathered in the Gitabitan.

Banglapedia groups them as devotional (Puja), love (Prem), seasons and nature (Prakriti), patriotic (Swadesh), occasional (Anusthanik) and miscellaneous (Vichitra), and says these divisions overlap. Occasional songs were written for weddings, funerals, tree planting and harvests.

The tunes draw on many sources: Brahmo devotional songs, Hindustani music, South Indian tunes, Bengali folk forms such as Baul and kirtan, and Western melodies. Banglapedia notes he often joined several ragas in one song, valued the theme over the raga, and used unusual tals.
artist: Tagore taught songs to students at Santiniketan. The Sangeet Bhavana at Visva-Bharati helped set how the songs are taught, and created a line of singers who specialise in them (Wikipedia).
Wikipedia names well-known interpreters: Kanika Banerjee, Suchitra Mitra, Pankaj Mullick, Hemant Kumar, Debabrata Biswas, Manna Dey, Shyamal Mitra, Santidev Ghosh and Sagar Sen, among others.
Two anthems come from his songs: India's Jana Gana Mana, adopted in 1950 after a first singing in 1911, and Bangladesh's Amar Shonar Bangla.
place: Santiniketan in Birbhum is where Tagore founded his school, which became Visva-Bharati. Kolkata, his family's home city, is where many of the songs were first sung, for instance at the Jorasanko house.
The songs are now sung across the Bengali world, in West Bengal and Bangladesh, and abroad.

history.what: Sources differ on when he began, either about age 12 or in 1875.
Songs from these years show his use of folk and devotional styles.
During the agitation against the partition of Bengal he drew heavily on Baul tunes.
The term Rabindra Sangeet is introduced for his 70th birthday anthology.
Tagore's last birthday and death. Songs continue to be published by Visva-Bharati.
Visva-Bharati has published 63 Gitabitan volumes with notation, with more planned (Banglapedia).

future: Training: teach tunes from the notation in the Gitabitan, not only from recordings.
Livelihood: support teachers and accompanists in small towns.
Materials: keep handmade instruments, such as the esraj, in use.
Documentation: complete and share the notation volumes, and record old singers.
Protection: respect the poem and the composed tune together, as Tagore wished.

name: Santhal Baha Songs
tagline: Songs of the sal-flower festival, sung in circles around the sacred grove.
facts: Songs of the Baha (flower) spring festival
Called Baha Sereng in Santali
Held at the Jaher, the sacred grove
Drums: madal and tamak
art: Baha is the spring festival of the Santhal, Ho and Munda peoples. The word means flower. Wikipedia describes the priest, the naike, offering sal flowers and leaves at the Jaherthan, then going door to door to bless each house. After the rituals come songs and dances.

The songs are called Baha Sereng. In a personal account, Phulmani Murmu writes that women sing Baha songs while moving in concentric circles. Drums, the madal and tamak, are central, according to Wikipedia.
We could not open a source that sets out the words or music of Baha songs, so this entry does not describe them in detail.
artist: The singers are the community: women, men and children of the village. The naike leads the ritual. Phulmani Murmu, a student, writes about helping her mother prepare the festival food and about the evening visits to the Jaher in traditional dress.
We found no source naming individual Baha singers, so none are named.
place: Baha is celebrated in Santhal villages of Jharkhand and in Birbhum, West Bengal, according to Wikipedia. The Jaher is the sacred grove where the community gathers. Murmu says offerings are made there to the ancestors, and Wikipedia names the deity Jaher Era (Jaher Ayo).
The festival comes in spring, and one search summary places it in the Bengali month of Falgun (February to March). This needs checking in a primary source.

history.what: We found no dated history of the songs. The festival itself is described as marking the start of the Santhal year in some sources, which we could not confirm in a page we read.
Murmu writes that she has not been able to celebrate Baha since the pandemic, living far from her village. Her account points to how migration affects the festival.

future: Record Baha Sereng with village singers, with the Santali words, in a community-owned archive.
Teach the songs and the madal and tamak to children in Santhal villages and schools.
Pay drum makers and players fairly, and secure hides and wood for the drums.
Protect the sacred grove so the Jaher stays in use.
Help Santhal families living away from home join the festival.

name: Sitar and Sarod
tagline: Two string instruments of Hindustani music, one with raised frets and a buzzing bridge, the other fretless with a metal fingerboard.
facts: Sitar: about 18 to 21 strings, with 6 or 7 played and the rest sympathetic
Sarod: fretless, metal fingerboard, goat-skin face
Miraj instrument cluster received a GI tag in 2024
Origins of both are debated; the Amir Khusrau story is doubted by scholars
art: The sitar and the sarod are the two best-known plucked string instruments of Hindustani classical music. Both are played by a soloist who builds a raga slowly, usually with a tabla player beside them.

A sitar has a long neck with curved, raised metal frets that can be moved for tuning. Wikipedia says it has 18 to 21 strings: six or seven are played, and the rest lie under the frets and ring in sympathy. A shaped bridge called the jawari gives the sitar its buzzing, shimmering tone. The body is a gourd, and the neck is usually of teak or tun wood. Players pull the melody string sideways across the frets to slide between notes, a technique called meend.

The sarod has no frets. Its fingerboard is a smooth metal plate, and the player stops the strings with the nails and fingertips of the left hand. The face of the body is covered in goat skin. Wikipedia says a conventional sarod has about 17 to 25 strings, including melody, drone, chikari and sympathetic strings. The sound is deep and rounded, and notes can be slid and held.

Where the instruments came from is not settled. A popular story says the poet Amir Khusrau invented the sitar in the 13th century. The Wikipedia article says scholars regard this as discredited, and that the earliest known mention is in a 1739 text from Delhi. Historians generally credit a figure of the 18th-century Mughal world with developing it from the Persian setar. For the sarod, scholars link it to the Afghan rabab and other older instruments. One account credits the Bangash family of musicians. More recent scholarship, cited on the same page, credits Niamatullah Khan of Lucknow, a rabab player at the court of Wajid Ali Shah. These accounts conflict, and we have not tried to settle them.
artist: Sitar and sarod playing is passed on through gharanas, families and schools of teaching, from teacher to student over many years. One of the best-known teachers was Allauddin Khan (c. 1881-1972). He was born in what is now Bangladesh and lived in Maihar, in present-day Madhya Pradesh, from 1918 until his death. His home there served as a gurukul. His students included Ravi Shankar, his son Ali Akbar Khan, his daughter Annapurna Devi, and Nikhil Banerjee. Wikipedia lists his honours, including the Sangeet Natak Akademi Fellowship in 1954 and the Padma Vibhushan in 1971.

Ravi Shankar took the sitar to wide audiences from the late 1950s and 1960s. Vilayat Khan developed a style that imitates the singing voice, in which the melody string is pulled to glide between notes. Ali Akbar Khan and Amjad Ali Khan are among the best-known sarod players. Amjad Ali Khan's family is said by one account to descend from the Bangash line, though that account is disputed.

Behind each performer is a maker. A good sitar or sarod is built for the individual player, and the bridge and gourd shape the sound. The makers are rarely named on concert programmes, and their story is part of this entry.
place: The two instruments belong to many places. Sources link early sarod history to Lucknow, Shahjahanpur, Gwalior and Rewa in the 1850s, and its later growth to Maihar under Allauddin Khan and to Kolkata. Delhi and Lucknow are tied to the sitar's early years.

Miraj, in Sangli district of southern Maharashtra, is the best-known centre of making. Sahapedia says the Shikalgar community, metalsmiths who repaired weapons, came to Miraj under the Adil Shahis in the 17th century. When their old trade declined they turned to other work. Faridsaheb Sitarmaker (1827-1898) is considered the founding father of the town's instrument making. Today's makers are said to be the seventh generation, working in a single lane. Sahapedia notes that instruments are made mostly by hand in small workshops.

In March 2024 the Miraj Musical Instruments Cluster received a Geographical Indication tag for sitars, and a firm called Soultune received one for tanpuras. The Week reports more than 450 craftsmen and a monthly output of 60 to 70 sitars. Other sources give lower numbers, so we treat the figure as approximate.

history.what: A story credits Amir Khusrau with inventing the sitar. Scholars cited on Wikipedia do not accept this, as no record of the name 'sitar' exists from his time.
The earliest known mention of the sitar appears in the Muraqqa-e-Dehli, written in the reign of Muhammad Shah.
Shikalgar metalsmiths settle in Miraj under the Adil Shahis, according to Sahapedia.
The sarod in its present form is recognised in Rewa, Shahjahanpur, Gwalior and Lucknow, according to Wikipedia. Metal strings and a metal plate are added in the later 19th century.
Faridsaheb Sitarmaker of Miraj lives and builds up the town's instrument trade, according to Sahapedia.
Allauddin Khan settles in Maihar as court musician and begins to teach there.
Ravi Shankar brings the sitar to audiences abroad.
Miraj sitars and tanpuras receive GI tags.

future: Support Miraj families and other makers with apprentices, so the know-how that lives in hands, not books, is passed on.
Name makers in concert notes and recordings, next to the players.
Document how a sitar and a sarod are built, step by step, in video with the makers' own words.
Help makers find fair prices and steady orders through the GI tag, and guard against fake 'Miraj' instruments.
Keep gurukul-style teaching affordable, so students from families without musical backgrounds can train.

name: Sufi Music of India
tagline: Songs of longing for the divine, sung at shrines where the music is part of the prayer.
facts: Qawwali is the best-known form
Sung at dargahs such as Nizamuddin in Delhi and Ajmer Sharif
Amir Khusrau is widely credited with shaping qawwali; this is presented as tradition
A party is usually 8 to 9 men: a lead, side singers, harmonium, percussion and a clapping chorus
art: Sufi music is the devotional music of Sufis, the mystical tradition of Islam. In India its best-known form is qawwali. Wikipedia calls qawwali the best-known form of Sufi music. It is sung at shrines to bring about remembrance of God and a state of spiritual ecstasy.

A qawwali party is usually eight or nine men: a lead singer, side singers, harmonium players, percussionists and a chorus that repeats the refrain and claps. A performance often begins with an instrumental prelude and a slow, unmetred opening. Then the main song begins with tabla, dholak and clapping and builds in speed, often with sargam passages, and ends suddenly.

The words come in many forms. Wikipedia lists hamd (praise of God), naat (praise of the Prophet), manqabat (praise of saints), ghazal and kafi. The songs speak of love and longing, often through images of wine and the beloved, which serve as mystical symbols.

The history is a story of contest. Wikipedia says the development of qawwali is widely attributed to Amir Khusrau, a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, who set it in the frame of the raga. It also notes that early Sufi authorities, including Nizamuddin, are reported to have opposed musical instruments, so early sama was sung without them. Instruments such as the harmonium and tabla came later.
artist: Qawwals often belong to families who have sung at a shrine for generations, but we name no individual qawwals because the sources we opened name none for India.

Baba Farid (c. 1188-1266), a founding figure of the Chishti order, was the teacher of Nizamuddin Auliya, according to Wikipedia. His verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, though some scholars argue part of them may be by a later Farid, according to Wikipedia. His shrine is in Pakpattan, in present-day Pakistan.
Many singers today perform in concerts and films as well as at shrines. A reader of this entry should hear the shrine singers where they sing, with respect for the setting.
place: Qawwali is tied to the dargahs of the Chishti order. The dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi is closely linked to the Sufi gatherings where qawwali took shape. Sahapedia has a short video of qawwali at the dargah. Ajmer Sharif in Rajasthan is another major shrine.

Sufi music is also found elsewhere in India: in Kashmir, in Punjab, and in the Deccan. We did not find a source we could open for these regions, so the pins mark only Delhi, Ajmer and Srinagar (approx.), and the entry stays short.

history.what: Nizamuddin Auliya, a Chishti saint in Delhi, holds gatherings of sama in his khanqah. His disciple Amir Khusrau is widely credited with shaping qawwali.
Baba Farid, a founding figure of the Chishti order, lives and teaches.
Instruments such as the sarangi, then the harmonium, tabla and dholak enter qawwali.
Qawwali is sung at shrines in India and also on stage, in film and on record.

future: Support families of shrine qawwals, whose numbers and audiences are said to be shrinking, with stipends and teaching places.
Document shrine repertoires, including Hindi, Urdu, Persian and Punjabi verses, with the singers' consent.
Keep the connection to shrine and community alive, rather than only on stage.
Record Sufi traditions beyond qawwali in Kashmir and other regions with local scholars.
Make the history of the Chishti and other Sufi orders accessible to younger listeners in plain language.

name: Sufiana Kalam and Santoor
tagline: A hundred strings, Persian maqams and Sufi verse: Kashmir's own classical music.
facts: Also called Sufiana Mausiqi
Uses Persian maqams instead of ragas
Ensemble of five to twelve singers with santoor, sehtar and others
Santoor: about a hundred strings struck with wooden mallets
art: Sufiana Kalam, usually called Sufiana Mausiqi, is the classical music of Kashmir. A group of five to twelve musicians sings Sufi poetry in Persian and Kashmiri, with santoor, Kashmiri sehtar, Saaz-e-Kashmir and a hand drum. The Jammu and Kashmir Policy Institute says it uses Persian maqams in place of ragas.

The Policy Institute describes how a piece goes. It opens with a shakal, an instrumental prelude often played on the santoor by the leader. A short unmetered recitation, the nasr, follows, using couplets of Lalleshwari. Then comes the first poem. Each verse is tied to a maqam and a tala cycle, beginning with the longest.

The santoor is a hammer-played zither. Enca describes it as having a hundred strings and being the core instrument of this music. Sahapedia says it was perfected in Srinagar's workshops. Religion Unplugged reports 62 modes in the repertoire and gives the music a Persian origin, but sources do not agree on numbers, and all agree that the repertoire has shrunk.
It is music of listening more than show. It is sung at gatherings, often at dusk, and at shrines and mehfils.
artist: Sahapedia names families and teachers. It mentions the gharanas of Shams Faqir and Ghulam Mohammad Qaleenbaaf, Ustad Ghulam Mohammad Saznawaz, Ustad Mohammad Yaqoob Sheikh, who mentors young musicians, and the santoor player Abdul Ghani Namtahali. The Policy Institute names Mushtaq Ahmad Saaznawaz, a seventh-generation member of the Saaznawaz family of Danamazar, Safakadal, who trains youth for free.

Pandit Bhajan Sopori, a santoor maestro and composer, said the decline came mostly from lost patronage and little money in the art, as the Policy Institute reports. Religion Unplugged says training takes about 25 years.

The instrument has its makers too. Enca writes about Ghulam Mohammad Zaz of Srinagar, an eighth-generation santoor maker who makes eight to ten instruments a year, and who says he has no guarantee anyone will carry on after him.
Shivkumar Sharma, born in Jammu and Kashmir in 1938, took the santoor into Hindustani classical music in the 1950s, says Enca. That made the instrument known across India.
place: The tradition took root in Srinagar, Sahapedia says, with mehfils held in wooden havelis and at Sufi shrines such as Khanqah-e-Moula. Anantnag is also named, where a music professor at a government college speaks about the tradition's history.

The Valley's shrine culture and its link with Persia are the backdrop. Sahapedia credits the saint Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani with bringing it, and the Policy Institute places its growth under Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin in the 15th century. Enca quotes a local professor who says Iranian musicians brought the instrument and Persian singing, and local musicians adapted them.

history.what: Sahapedia says the tradition took root in Srinagar by this time and credits Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani. Religion Unplugged also says it came from Persia in the 14th century.
The Policy Institute says it developed under Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (about 1420-1470).

Hafiz Nagma, a dance in which a woman showed the meaning of the song through gesture, was once paired with Sufiana. The Policy Institute says it later died out, though it was reportedly still part of the ensemble as late as 1920.
Royal and maharaja patronage ended and the music moved into private gatherings and shrines, according to the Policy Institute.
Shivkumar Sharma brought the santoor into Hindustani classical music, says Enca.
The Religion Unplugged report says Radio Kashmir's musician posts have gone unfilled since 1992.

Sahapedia notes events such as the Shashrang Festival and performances at the Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture and Languages that have renewed interest. Enca's source reports that young people are again learning traditional instruments, a modest trend.

future: Training: teach Sufiana in schools from an early age, with scholarships, as experts quoted by the Policy Institute suggest.
Livelihood: give musicians steady paid work, such as posts at the radio and the Academy, since lost income is blamed for the decline.
Materials: support santoor and sehtar makers, who are few. Pay for apprentices.
Documentation: record the surviving maqams and talas and the Saaz-e-Kashmir, which Policy Institute calls nearly extinct.
Protection: open the teaching more widely, including to daughters' children and to girls, since some ustads kept knowledge closed.

name: Tabla
tagline: A pair of hand drums that speaks in syllables and keeps time for song, dance and instrument.
facts: Two drums: the dayan (right, treble) and the bayan (left, bass)
The black syahi paste on each head shapes the bell-like tone
Six commonly named gharanas: Delhi, Lucknow, Ajrara, Farrukhabad, Benares, Punjab
The story that Amir Khusrau split a pakhawaj is not supported by evidence
art: The tabla is a pair of hand drums. The smaller, right-hand drum is the dayan, made of wood such as teak or rosewood and tuned to a note of the raga. The larger left-hand drum is the bayan, usually made of brass, with copper considered the best. Each head has a round black patch in the middle called the syahi, made from layers of starch paste mixed with black powder. Wikipedia calls it the main factor in the quality of the instrument.

The drums are tuned with leather straps, wooden blocks called gatta, and a small hammer. The dayan is tuned to a precise note. The bayan is a bass voice, and the pressure of the heel of the left hand changes its pitch while it sounds.

Each stroke has a spoken syllable, called a bol, such as na, tin, ge and dha. Tabla is taught by speaking the bols first and then playing them. Two main written systems exist, those of Paluskar and Bhatkhande. A player may accompany a singer, a dancer or an instrumentalist, or play a solo.

The origin of the drum is debated. One view links it to older Indian drums and cites carvings at Bhaja caves from about the 2nd century BCE. Another links it to Muslim and Mughal influence, from the Arabic word tabl, meaning drum. The popular story that Amir Khusrau split a pakhawaj in two to make the tabla has no evidence from his time. Wikipedia cites the scholars Neil Sorrell and Ram Narayan, who say it cannot be given any credence. Clear pictures of the drum appear only from about 1745.
artist: Tabla playing is handed down within gharanas, each with its own repertoire and finger technique. Wikipedia lists six commonly named ones: Delhi, Lucknow, Ajrara, Farrukhabad, Benares and Punjab. Modern travel and recording have softened the boundaries between them.

Wikipedia says the Benares gharana was founded by Pandit Ram Sahai (1780-1826), who trained in Lucknow. After a performance in Benares he is said to have shut himself away for six months and developed the new style. Farrukhabad, according to a page that itself lacks citations, was named after the town where Vilayat Ali Khan (1779-1826) lived. Sources differ on who founded it first.

Players named on the Wikipedia tabla page include Ahmed Jan Thirakwa, Alla Rakha, Kishan Maharaj, Zakir Hussain, Anindo Chatterjee and Swapan Chaudhuri. Many accompanists have shaped the music without a solo name, and a good tabla player is one who listens to the main performer.
place: Tabla grew up in the cities of north India. Delhi is usually named as the oldest gharana, dated to the early 18th century. Farrukhabad, Lucknow and Benares are grouped as the purbi baj, the eastern style. Ajrara is in the Meerut region of Uttar Pradesh. Our pins show Delhi, Lucknow, Farrukhabad, Varanasi and Mumbai.
Today the drum is played across India and abroad, in Hindustani concerts, in Kathak, in bhajan and ghazal, and in film music.

history.what: Carvings at the Bhaja caves are cited by one school of thought as evidence for early Indian drum pairs.
The Amir Khusrau story, which scholars say lacks contemporary evidence.
Clear pictorial evidence of the tabla appears.
The Delhi gharana, the oldest, takes shape.
Ram Sahai develops the Benares style, according to Wikipedia.
Farrukhabad, Lucknow and other gharanas build their repertoires.
Tabla becomes a concert solo instrument and is heard outside India.

future: Support gharana families and senior players to teach, and to record whole compositions as well as short clips.
Support the makers who prepare the syahi and the drum shells, whose names rarely appear.
Teach the bol notation in schools along with the spoken syllables, so students learn both.
Document each gharana's compositions with the family's consent, in an open archive.
Ensure that young players from outside hereditary families have access to good teachers.

name: Thanjavur Veena
tagline: A lute carved from jackfruit wood, the first Indian musical instrument said to hold a GI tag.
facts: Wood: jackfruit, seasoned
Two types: ekanda (one piece) and ottu (joined)
GI: registered 2012-13 per most sources; one report says 2010
Weight: about 7 to 8 kg, per DT Next
art: The Thanjavur veena is a type of Saraswati veena from the Thanjavur region. It is about 4 feet long, with a round wooden resonator (kudam), a thick long neck and a carved end (yali head). It has four playing strings and three side drone strings, and 24 fixed metal frets set in wax mixed with charcoal powder, according to Wikipedia.

It is made from jackfruit wood, cut, dried and carved. Makers prefer wood from mature trees for its fine pores and lasting strength. DT Next says a veena has three parts: peg box, fingerboard and resonator. If all three come from one log, it is called ekanda (or ekantha). If made separately and joined, it is ottu (or sada). Both are made in Thanjavur.

Making a good instrument needs a feel for sound as well as for wood. A Thanjavur maker told DT Next that makers need to know music and the quality of tone. The same article says the veena is the lightest of its kind and gives a weight of 7 to 8 kg.

Wikipedia and other pages call it the first musical instrument in India to get a GI tag. That claim is disputed: the Bobbili veena of Andhra Pradesh is also reported to have received GI status in March 2012, so which came first depends on the exact date. The Thanjavur year also varies in sources, 2010 in DT Next, and 2012-13 elsewhere. The GI registry should be checked directly.
artist: The sources I read name only one maker, T. Gunasekaran of South Street, Thanjavur, quoted by DT Next in January 2024. He says orders come from the US, Canada, Singapore and Malaysia and asks for government help with exports.

DT Next says only about 40 people still make the traditional veena, down from a larger skilled workforce that left for other work when patronage fell. It also says monthly sales have risen from 50 to 60 veenas to over 100, because parents want their children, especially girls, to learn the instrument.
I did not find a source naming specific hereditary families, so none are named here. A fuller study of Thanjavur's veena-making households is still needed.

The players are a separate story. The Tanjore Quartet were four brothers at the court of the Maratha king Serfoji II: Chinnayya (1802 to 1856), Ponnayya (1804 to 1864), Sivanandam (1808 to 1863) and Vadivelu (1810 to 1845, though one source gives 1847). They are famous for Bharatanatyam and music, and one source calls Sivanandam a veena player. They show how Thanjavur's court shaped Carnatic arts, but the sources I read do not link them to veena making.
place: Thanjavur lies in the Cauvery delta, in Tamil Nadu, and was a great seat of art under the Nayaks and the Marathas. The Tamil Nadu Tourism page on the veena says the shape was fixed under the Nayak rulers, and DT Next says it was finalised in the early 17th century in the time of King Raghunatha Nayak. Both statements come from tradition and are not a documented date.
The wood has become a problem. DT Next says Thanjavur once had many jackfruit trees but the number has fallen, so makers now buy wood from Panruti and Cuddalore.

Tiruvaiyaru, on the Cauvery near Thanjavur, is the town where the composer Thyagaraja lived, and it is known for a yearly music festival in his memory. I did not find a source that ties the veena workshops to Tiruvaiyaru, so I mention the town only as a nearby music centre.
Thanjavur is also known for other crafts, such as bronze casting and Tanjore painting (see separate entry), which share the city's workshop skills and temple patronage.

history.what: The veena is an old stringed instrument; Wikipedia says it is mentioned in the Vedas. Forms changed over the centuries.
The modern Thanjavur veena shape is said to be fixed in the reign of Raghunatha Nayak.
The Tanjore Quartet serve at the Maratha court of Serfoji II in Thanjavur.
The Thanjavur veena is registered as a GI. Sources differ on the year.
The Bobbili veena is also reported to have received GI status, so the 'first instrument' claim is contested.
About 40 makers remain, and demand for children's lessons is rising, according to DT Next (2024).

future: Plant and protect jackfruit trees around Thanjavur and set up a managed wood-seasoning yard for makers.
Set up an apprenticeship scheme so the few remaining makers can train young carvers with a stipend.
Help makers sell abroad with clear export rules and shipping help.
Document ekanda carving step by step on film with senior makers, and name the families.
Use the GI to certify genuine Thanjavur veenas, with the maker's name on each instrument.
Offer school music programmes where children also see how the instrument is made.

name: Villupattu
tagline: A story sung to the twang of a great bow resting on a clay pot.
facts: Form: sung storytelling with a bow, pot, drum and cymbals
Name means bow song (vil = bow, pattu = song)
Heard at village temple festivals in Tirunelveli and Kanyakumari
Few full-time practitioners remain
art: Villupattu, or bow song, is a form of musical storytelling from the far south of Tamil Nadu. The lead singer plays a long bow called the villu or vil. It gives the art its name.

The bow rests on the neck of a clay pot. A second performer beats the pot while singing, and a co-singer answers the narrator and keeps the story moving. Other instruments listed on the ARCE exhibition page, from the Nazir Jairazbhoy collection, include the hourglass drum (udukkai), wooden blocks (kattai), the pot (kutam) and cymbals.

The stories range from gods and goddesses to local heroes. Bow-song texts recorded by the scholar Stuart Blackburn include the tales of Vallarakkan, linked to the birth of the deity Sasta, of Muthupattan, and of the Little Brothers, Kunju Thampi and Valiya Thampi, who die in the story. Other accounts say troupes also sing from the Ramayana and Mahabharata and of local goddesses.
The songs are sung in village temples during festivals such as the Kotai festival. Singing is traditionally seen as a sacred act, not only entertainment.
artist: Villupattu is a team art. The lead singer carries the bow, and the troupe supports with pot, drum, cymbals and responses. Many performers learned inside their own communities and sang at festivals for deities such as Sudalai Madan and Mutharamman.

One well-known performer was Poongani of Kottaram village in Kanyakumari district. The News Minute reports that she began at the age of 10, inspired by twin sisters who played the bow, and says she was only the third woman to perform villupattu. She led a troupe of men and performed for more than fifty years, until about the age of 70.

The same report says she had not received the state's Kalaimamani award, reportedly because her performances were not documented. It describes her living on a small pension. Her story shows how much depends on recording this art and on supporting its singers.
place: The tradition is centred on the southernmost districts of Tamil Nadu, Tirunelveli and Kanyakumari. The ARCE exhibition places the festival performances in many village temples across these two districts.

Wikipedia adds that the form is also found in southern Kerala and north-east Sri Lanka, and that the Kerala bow instrument, villadivadyam, has its own form. Kottaram, home of Poongani, lies in Kanyakumari district.

history.what: Stuart Blackburn, as reported by secondary sources, notes mentions of a singing bow in very old Tamil literature. Clear evidence of the bow song tradition itself appears much later.
Sources date the development of the tradition differently, so the period is uncertain.
Photographs show bow-song musicians performing in the 19th century.
Troupes sang at temple festivals across Tirunelveli and Kanyakumari. Poongani's career ran for over fifty years.
Fieldwork by Stuart Blackburn recorded about 175 hours of bow song audio over eighteen months. A part of it is now online at the ARCE archive.
Reports say the number of practising artists has fallen because performing rarely pays enough to live on.

future: Support training for young singers, including women, under experienced bow singers.
Pay fair fees for festival and stage performances so the art can be a livelihood.
Keep making and repairing the villu and pot with local craftspeople.
Record and archive full performances, and credit the singers by name.
Recognise senior performers with honours and pensions while they can still enjoy them.
